High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction

Saksham Jain Affiliation: University of Washington    Guillaume Braun Affiliation: RIKEN AIP    Masaaki Imaizumi Affiliation: University of Tokyo Affiliation: RIKEN AIP Affiliation: Kyoto University
Abstract

Reward models used for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are commonly selected using held-out data. When sample size and context dimension grow proportionally, the difference in test risk between models fitted on the full sample and on a fixed fraction of it need not vanish. Held-out evaluation can therefore consistently estimate the test risk of the model trained on the smaller sample, but because the relative ranking of candidate reward models can change after full-data refitting, held-out selection can be suboptimal. We develop an Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion that estimates the full-data reward model’s out-of-sample risk under the target policy using only its training observations. This enables early stopping along the full-data gradient-descent trajectory without sample splitting. For neural networks with fixed depth and hidden width under Gaussian contexts, single-index rewards, context-dependent multi-index target policies, and known context-independent logging, we prove uniform consistency of our criterion over a fixed finite set of gradient-descent iterates and a near-oracle guarantee for the selected reward model. The same correction yields a doubly robust estimator that consistently estimates the true policy value without sample splitting, even when reward-model prediction error does not vanish. Experiments show decreasing risk-estimation error as dimension grows at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, and improved reward-model selection relative to held-out baselines. Empirically, our correction also reduces the root mean squared error of doubly robust value estimates computed from the same data used to fit and select the reward models.

   

November 5, 2026

1 Introduction

Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value of a target policy from data collected by a different logging policy. In contextual bandits, only the rewards of the logged actions are observed, so evaluating a new policy requires estimating its expected reward from partial feedback. Many OPE estimators therefore rely on learned reward models to predict unobserved rewards (Beygelzimer and Langford, 2009; Dudík et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017; Farajtabar et al., 2018). The out-of-sample performance of these models matters for value estimation (Su et al., 2020a; Metelli et al., 2021) and for related decision-making tasks such as policy optimization (Dudík et al., 2014; Athey and Wager, 2021) and staged online bandit learning (Kang et al., 2026; Ma and Cai, 2025; Arya et al., 2026). Selecting a reward model with good prediction performance under the target policy is therefore an important part of OPE.

A natural approach is to select a reward model using held-out prediction error or cross-validation, with importance weighting when appropriate, and then refit it on the full logged sample (Arlot and Celisse, 2010; Sugiyama et al., 2007). Although the held-out criterion estimates the test risk of the model trained on the remaining observations, it does not directly estimate the test risk of the model obtained after refitting (Bates et al., 2024). This distinction is particularly important in proportional high-dimensional regimes, where sample size and context dimension grow proportionally and prediction risk can depend nontrivially on the sample-to-dimension ratio (Dobriban and Wager, 2018; Han and Xu, 2024; Han and Imaizumi, 2025). Holding out a fixed fraction changes this ratio, so the difference between the full-data and reduced-sample models’ test risks need not vanish.

Estimating full-data test risk from training observations requires accounting for each observation’s influence on its own fitted prediction (Bellec and Tan, 2026; Han and Imaizumi, 2025). In the proportional regime, this influence can persist, so the importance-weighted training error need not consistently estimate test risk. The same dependence can make a doubly robust (DR) policy-value estimator inconsistent when evaluated on its reward model’s training data. For instance, Proposition 4.3 shows that this can occur after a single gradient-descent step. We therefore ask:

Can one train and select a reward model on the full logged sample,
and consistently estimate policy value from the same sample?

We answer this affirmatively for neural reward models trained by full-batch gradient descent. Building on state-evolution theory for first-order methods (Han, 2025; Bellec and Tan, 2026) and the neural Onsager correction of Han and Imaizumi (2025), we construct an in-sample criterion that estimates target-policy-weighted out-of-sample error. The primary technical challenge of this paper is importance weighting: the target-to-logging ratio depends on the same covariates as the learned representation, so its dependence on the prediction error must be retained. We augment the state evolution to jointly track the linear projections that determine the target-policy probabilities and the learned hidden states. The corrected predictions are used both to select the stopping gradient descent iterate and to form ‘adjusted’ direct and doubly robust value estimates.

We study single-index rewards, where each arm’s mean reward is an unknown function of a one-dimensional projection of the context. Our analysis in the proportional asymptotics regime assumes Gaussian contexts, known context-independent logging, and neural networks of fixed depth and width. Our contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We construct an Onsager-corrected criterion and prove that it consistently estimates the target-policy-weighted conditional test risk of neural reward models trained via gradient descent on the full logged sample.

  2. 2.

    We show that using this criterion for reward model selection yields near-optimal early stopping without sample splitting for hold-out or cross validation.

  3. 3.

    We establish guarantees for value-estimation on the full logged sample by using the Onsager-corrected criterion to construct adjusted value estimators that are consistent for their true population targets, without sample splitting, cross-fitting, or requiring prediction error relative to the true reward model to vanish.

  4. 4.

    We demonstrate the benefits of our methods empirically: at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, our criterion’s risk-estimation error and selection regret decrease as dimension grows. When sample size outgrows dimension, our adjusted doubly robust estimator attains a mean squared error close to the classical semiparametric efficiency benchmark at the largest sample size studied.

A detailed discussion of related work is provided in Appendix A.

2 Statistical Framework

2.1 Problem Formulation

OPE in contextual bandit settings.

We observe an i.i.d. sample 𝒟m≔{Qi}i=1m\mathcal{D}_{m}\coloneqq\{Q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} collected under a context-independent logging policy μ\mu. Each observation Qi=(Xi,Ai,Ri)∈ℝd×[K]×ℝQ_{i}=(X_{i},A_{i},R_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[K]\times\mathbb{R} with K≥2K\geq 2 comprises the context, the logged action, and the resulting reward. We assume the standard positivity condition (Dudík et al., 2014): μ⁡(a)≥c>0\mu(a)\geq c>0 for every a∈[K]a\in[K]. We assume rewards are generated as Ri≔g∗​(Xi,Ai)+εiR_{i}\coloneqq g^{\ast}(X_{i},A_{i})+\varepsilon_{i} with some g∗:ℝd×[K]→ℝg^{\ast}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[K]\to\mathbb{R}, where, conditional on Ai=aA_{i}=a, the noise εi∈ℝ\varepsilon_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is independent of XiX_{i}, mean-zero, and has finite variance. We wish to evaluate a fixed target policy ν\nu, specified independently of the logged sample and allowed to depend on the contexts. Let ν⁡(a∣x)\nu(a\mid x) denote the probability of choosing action aa given context xx. The value of the target policy ν\nu is defined as:

𝒱⁡(ν)≔𝔼Pν​[R]=𝔼PX​𝔼νA|X​𝔼PR|A,X​[R]=𝔼⁡[∑a=1Kν⁡(a|X)​g∗​(X,a)].\mathcal{V}(\nu)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{P_{\nu}}[R]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{X}}\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{A\,|\,X}}\mathbb{E}_{P_{R\,|\,A,X}}[R]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X)g^{\ast}(X,a)\right]. (1)

Here the final expectation is over the marginal distribution of XX. To make the dependence on the true reward function explicit, we also write this value as 𝒱g∗​(ν)\mathcal{V}_{g^{\ast}}(\nu). For any fixed measurable reward model g:ℝd×[K]→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[K]\to\mathbb{R} satisfying 𝔼⁡[∑aν⁡(a∣X)​|g⁡(X,a)|]<∞\mathbb{E}[\sum_{a}\nu(a\mid X)|g(X,a)|]<\infty, define 𝒱g​(ν)\mathcal{V}_{g}(\nu) by replacing g∗g^{\ast} with gg in the final expression above. This is the population quantity estimated by the direct method (DM) (Beygelzimer and Langford, 2009; Dudík et al., 2014).

Importance-weighted risk as selection criterion.

Let wa​(x):=ν⁡(a|x)/μ⁡(a)w_{a}(x):=\nu(a\,|\,x)/\mu(a) be the target-to-logging importance ratio (Sugiyama et al., 2007; Farajtabar et al., 2018) for arm aa, and observe that since ν(⋅|x)\nu(\cdot\,|\,x) is a distribution, wa​(x)≥0w_{a}(x)\geq 0 and ∑aμ⁡(a)​wa​(x)=1\sum_{a}\mu(a)w_{a}(x)=1 for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We distinguish the reward model’s squared error relative to the true reward function, ℛν∘​(g)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g), from its squared error in predicting a new reward, ℛν​(g)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g). Averaging under the target policy, we define these quantities as

ℛν∘​(g)≔𝔼​∑a=1Kν⁡(a|X)​(g⁡(X,a)−g∗​(X,a))2,ℛν​(g)≔𝔼⁡[wA​(X)​(R−g⁡(X,A))2].\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X)\left(g(X,a)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\right)^{2},\quad\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\left(R-g(X,A)\right)^{2}\right]. (2)

For a single-arm predictor gag_{a}, let ℛν,a∘​(ga)≔𝔼⁡[ν⁡(a|X)​(ga​(X)−g∗​(X,a))2]\mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\nu(a\,|\,X)\left(g_{a}(X)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\right)^{2}]. Two facts make ℛν∘​(g)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g) useful for OPE. First, Cauchy–Schwarz gives |𝒱g​(ν)−𝒱⁡(ν)|2≤ℛν∘​(g)\left\lvert\mathcal{V}_{g}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right\rvert^{2}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g), so prediction error bounds the squared error in the model-induced policy value. Second, Proposition H.10 uses this prediction error to bound the additional variance of a DR score evaluated on an observation independent of model fitting, relative to the score using g∗g^{\ast}. These bounds motivate prediction risk as a selection objective; minimizing it need not minimize the value estimator’s mean squared error.

Although g∗g^{\ast} is unknown, the zero-mean independent noise assumption gives ℛν​(g)=𝔼⁡[wA​(X)​ε2]+ℛν∘​(g)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g)=\mathbb{E}[w_{A}(X)\varepsilon^{2}]+\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g). The noise term does not depend on gg, so minimizing test risk also minimizes prediction error over the same candidate models.

Our goal is to construct a model selector based on ℛν​(g)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g) and to use the selected reward model for policy value estimation, without sample splitting. Note that for learned predictors, all risk and value functionals are understood to be for an independent test draw, conditional on the training data and network initializations; these are defined formally in Appendix C.

Doubly robust value estimation.

For a reward model gg, the doubly robust score is defined as

ψg​(X,A,R)≔∑a=1Kν⁡(a∣X)​g​(X,a)+wA​(X)​{R−g⁡(X,A)}.\psi_{g}(X,A,R)\coloneqq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\mid X)g(X,a)+w_{A}(X)\{R-g(X,A)\}. (3)

Let PdP_{d} denote expectation over a new observation Q=(X,A,R)Q=(X,A,R) from the logging distribution, holding the reward model fixed; the subscript allows the data law to depend on dimension dd. For any fixed gg satisfying 𝔼⁡[∑aν⁡(a∣X)​|g⁡(X,a)|]<∞\mathbb{E}[\sum_{a}\nu(a\mid X)|g(X,a)|]<\infty, and assuming 𝔼⁡[wA​(X)​|R|]<∞\mathbb{E}[w_{A}(X)|R|]<\infty, conditioning on XX yields

𝔼⁡[ψg​(X,A,R)∣X]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\psi_{g}(X,A,R)\mid X] =∑a=1Kν⁡(a∣X)​g​(X,a)+∑a=1Kμ⁡(a)​wa​(X)​{g∗​(X,a)−g⁡(X,a)}=∑a=1Kν⁡(a∣X)​g∗​(X,a).\displaystyle=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\mid X)g(X,a)+\sum_{a=1}^{K}\mu(a)w_{a}(X)\{g^{\ast}(X,a)-g(X,a)\}=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\mid X)g^{\ast}(X,a).

Because the logging probabilities are known, Pd​ψg=𝒱⁡(ν)P_{d}\psi_{g}=\mathcal{V}(\nu) for every fixed reward model, even when g≠g∗g\neq g^{\ast} (setting g=0g=0 gives the inverse propensity scoring, or IPS, score). The identity also holds for a fitted model, provided the evaluation data is independent of the data used for fitting and selection.

Cross-fitting avoids the need for an additional evaluation sample by applying this identity on disjoint partitions of the data: each observation is evaluated using a model fitted and selected without its fold, so its score has a conditional mean of 𝒱⁡(ν)\mathcal{V}(\nu) given its training complement (Schick, 1986; Chernozhukov et al., 2018). Thus, with a fixed number of folds, and under suitable moment bounds (Chernozhukov et al., 2018), value estimation is consistent even when prediction error persists.

However, each reward model is consequently trained on a reduced sample, and reward model selection still matters for the precision of value estimation. When an inner validation split selects the model, it assesses models trained on fewer observations than the subsequent refit on the complete training complement. This training-size mismatch can make stopping-time selection suboptimal after refitting (see Appendix G). In Section 5, we compare this procedure with our corrected criterion, which selects directly on that complement.

An alternative is to reuse the full sample for training, selection, and evaluation and show that the resulting dependence has a negligible effect. Let Pm,dP_{m,d} be the empirical measure of the logged sample and let 𝔾m,d=m​(Pm,d−Pd)\mathbb{G}_{m,d}=\sqrt{m}(P_{m,d}-P_{d}). If g^\widehat{g} is fitted and selected on this sample, the same-sample DR estimator Pm,d​ψg^P_{m,d}\psi_{\widehat{g}} satisfies the exact decomposition

m​{Pm,d​ψg^−𝒱⁡(ν)}=m​{Pm,d​ψg^−Pd​ψg∗}=𝔾m,d​ψg∗+𝔾m,d​(ψg^−ψg∗).\sqrt{m}\{P_{m,d}\psi_{\widehat{g}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\}=\sqrt{m}\{P_{m,d}\psi_{\widehat{g}}-P_{d}\psi_{g^{\ast}}\}=\mathbb{G}_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}}+\mathbb{G}_{m,d}(\psi_{\widehat{g}}-\psi_{g^{\ast}}). (4)

The first term is the fluctuation of the score using the true reward function. The second is the empirical-process term that arises due to replacing g∗g^{\ast} with the fitted model g^\widehat{g}. Note that there is no population remainder because we assume known logging probabilities. If the second term is op​(1)o_{p}(1), fitting and selecting the model on the same observations as the evaluation data does not change the first-order behavior of estimator Pm,d​ψg^P_{m,d}\psi_{\widehat{g}} relative to Pm,d​ψg∗P_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}} at the m\sqrt{m} scale.

For a fixed distribution PP, the second term is op​(1)o_{p}(1) if ψg^\psi_{\widehat{g}} belongs with probability tending to one to a fixed PP-Donsker class and ∥ψg^−ψg∗∥L2​(P)→p0\|\psi_{\widehat{g}}-\psi_{g^{\ast}}\|_{L^{2}(P)}\to_{p}0 (Kennedy, 2024). Suitable algorithmic stability, together with nuisance convergence and regularity conditions, also permits asymptotically normal estimation without sample splitting (Chen et al., 2022).

These sufficient conditions are not automatic in our proportional regime. Indeed, prediction error need not vanish, and as we show in Appendix H.1, even a class of linear reward models with uniformly vanishing L2​(Pd)L^{2}(P_{d}) score errors can have a nonvanishing empirical-process supremum.

Rather than assuming the effect of sample reuse is negligible at first-order, we analyze the fitted reward models at candidate (for selection) gradient-descent iterates and apply an Onsager correction to their same-sample evaluation. Section 4.2 establishes consistency of our adjusted doubly robust (ADR) estimator (developed in Section 3.2) on the full training sample without requiring prediction error to vanish. It also shows why the correction matters: uncorrected same-sample DR estimation can be inconsistent after a single gradient-descent step.

2.2 Neural Reward Learning

We fit a separate reward model for each arm. For a∈[K]a\in[K], let ℐa≔{i∈[m]:Ai=a}\mathcal{I}_{a}\coloneqq\{i\in[m]:A_{i}=a\} be the indices of observations assigned to arm aa, with count Na≔|ℐa|N_{a}\coloneqq|\mathcal{I}_{a}|. Because logging is context-independent, conditioning on the action labels preserves the common context distribution within each arm. Each model is a feed-forward neural network of depth L≥2L\geq 2, hidden width q≥1q\geq 1, and scalar output. The learnable weight parameter is Wa=(Wa,1,Wa,[2:L])W_{a}=(W_{a,1},W_{a,[2:L]}), comprising the first layer Wa,1∈ℝd×qW_{a,1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q} and the deeper layers Wa,[2:L]W_{a,[2:L]}. The learned predictor is defined by:

fWa(x)≔GWa,[2:L](x⊤Wa,1),f_{W_{a}}(x)\coloneqq G_{W_{a,[2:L]}}\bigl(x^{\top}W_{a,1}\bigr),

where GWa,[2:L]:ℝq→ℝG_{W_{a,[2:L]}}:\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R} is the scalar feed-forward map defined by the deeper layers acting on the first-layer hidden state u=x⊤​Wa,1∈ℝqu=x^{\top}W_{a,1}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}. We identify hidden-state rows in ℝ1×q\mathbb{R}^{1\times q} with elements of ℝq\mathbb{R}^{q} when evaluating the network, and write gradients with respect to these coordinates as column vectors. We use smooth activations throughout. The collection of arm-wise initializations (Wa(0))a∈[K](W_{a}^{(0)})_{a\in[K]} is jointly independent of 𝒟m\mathcal{D}_{m}, with first-layer weights scaled by d−1/2d^{-1/2}. The prescribed deterministic layer-wise learning-rate schedule is denoted by {ηa,α(s):α∈[1:L],s≥0}\{\eta_{a,\alpha}^{(s)}:\alpha\in[1:L],s\geq 0\}, where α\alpha indexes network layers. Appendix C states the architecture, initialization, and regularity conditions, including the representation of the scalar output used to apply the state-evolution results.

Simultaneous full-batch gradient descent (GD) on every layer of the arm-wise squared loss

ℒa​(Wa)≔(2​Na)−1​∑i∈ℐa(Ri−fWa​(Xi))2\mathcal{L}_{a}(W_{a})\coloneqq(2N_{a})^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}\bigl(R_{i}-f_{W_{a}}(X_{i})\bigr)^{2}

produces iterates {Wa(t)}t∈𝒯\{W_{a}^{(t)}\}_{t\in\mathcal{T}} and fitted arm-wise models ga,t​(x)≔fWa(t)​(x)g_{a,t}(x)\coloneqq f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(x). For an iterate vector 𝐭=(t1,…,tK)∈𝒯K\mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{K})\in\mathcal{T}^{K}, we write g𝐭​(x,a)≔ga,ta​(x)g_{\mathbf{t}}(x,a)\coloneqq g_{a,t_{a}}(x).

We analyze this arm-wise reward learning in the high-dimensional proportional regime, where the aspect ratio m/d→ϕ∈(0,∞)m/d\to\phi\in(0,\infty) with the number of arms KK, network depth LL, width qq, and nonempty GD iterate grid 𝒯⊂ℤ≥0\mathcal{T}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} all finite and fixed. Unlike neural tangent kernel-type regimes, where representations remain close to initialization during training (Jacot et al., 2018; Bartlett et al., 2021), our finite-width setting allows non-trivial feature learning across multiple layers.

2.3 Assumptions

We make the following assumptions for our analysis. Most are standard regularity conditions used in finite-width state-evolution analyses, as in Han and Imaizumi (2025); we emphasize the assumptions that concern the OPE problem structure and target-policy weighting. The formal exposition of all conditions in this section, including on the true reward function and neural network architecture, is provided in Appendix C.

Assumption 2.1 (Known context-independent logging under positivity).

The logging policy is known and context-independent, with μ⁡(a)≥c>0\mu(a)\geq c>0 for every a∈[K]a\in[K], where cc is independent of dd.

Assumption 2.2 (Single-index rewards under Gaussian design).

The contexts satisfy Xi​∼i​i​d​𝒩​(0,Id)X_{i}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). For each arm aa, assume g∗​(x,a)=φa∗​(βa⊤​x)g^{\ast}(x,a)=\varphi_{a}^{\ast}(\beta_{a}^{\top}x) with ‖βa‖2=1\left\|\beta_{a}\right\|_{2}=1, d​‖βa‖∞=do⁡(1)\sqrt{d}\left\|\beta_{a}\right\|_{\infty}=d^{o(1)}, and φa∗\varphi_{a}^{\ast} smooth and of polynomial growth. We also let the arm-wise noise εi|Ai=a\varepsilon_{i}\,|\,A_{i}=a be sub-Gaussian with a dimension-independent parameter.

Assumption 2.3 (Multi-index importance weights).

We let waw_{a} be a multi-index function, i.e., wa​(x)=ha​(Υ⊤​x)w_{a}(x)=h_{a}(\Upsilon^{\top}x) with Υ=(γ1,…,γℓ)∈ℝd×ℓ\Upsilon=(\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{\ell})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times\ell}, Υ⊤​Υ=Iℓ\Upsilon^{\top}\Upsilon=I_{\ell}, d​‖γj‖∞≤CΥ\sqrt{d}\,\left\|\gamma_{j}\right\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\Upsilon} for each jj, and hah_{a} is nonnegative, bounded, and Lipschitz, with ∑aμ⁡(a)​ha​(u)=1\sum_{a}\mu(a)h_{a}(u)=1 for every u∈ℝℓu\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}, for some fixed ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. The coordinate bound and the common boundedness and Lipschitz constants are independent of dd.

Assumption 2.1 accommodates practically relevant logging policies such as pure exploration, randomized controlled trials and A/B tests. Our guarantees assume known logging probabilities. Under the proportional regime, this assumption ensures that the arm-wise aspect ratios ϕa=Na/d\phi_{a}=N_{a}/d belong to a fixed interval [c−,c+]⊂(0,∞)[c_{-},c_{+}]\subset(0,\infty) with probability tending to one. Proposition S.1 yields this count bound and the resulting reduction to arm-wise regression. Assumption 2.2 permits unknown nonlinear, arm-specific link functions—a setting of active interest in recent bandit literature (Kang et al., 2026; Ma and Cai, 2025; Arya et al., 2026). The isotropic Gaussian design is a standard, if restrictive, assumption in state evolution theory (Bayati and Montanari, 2011; Berthier et al., 2020; Bellec and Tan, 2026); extensions of the weighted comparison beyond Gaussian contexts are discussed in Section 6. Finally, sub-Gaussian noise is assumed merely for convenience; our proofs hold under milder moment and envelope conditions detailed in Appendix C. Assumption 2.3 includes e.g. logistic, softmax, and probit policies whose scores depend on a fixed number of linear projections satisfying the stated bounds. Different arms may use different projections, provided their joint span admits an orthonormal basis Υ\Upsilon satisfying the coordinate bounds above. For isotropic Gaussian contexts, Corollary C.3 permits arbitrary fixed reward and policy-index directions, including axis-aligned directions, under the stated data-independent initialization and size conditions.

3 Full-Sample OPE via Onsager Correction

This section introduces our full-sample OPE procedure based on the general first-order method (GFOM) Onsager correction (Bayati and Montanari, 2011; Celentano et al., 2020; Han and Xu, 2024; Han and Imaizumi, 2025). We first correct each training observation’s hidden state to account for its contribution to the fitted weights, removing the leading sample-reuse bias induced by gradient-based training. We then use the resulting predictions for model selection and for direct and doubly robust value estimation, without sample splitting.

3.1 GFOM-Corrected Hidden States

Our goal is to estimate the weighted test risk ℛν​(g)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g) (2) without a holdout set. We apply the GFOM correction separately to each arm’s fitted network. Fix an arm aa, and let Xa∈ℝNa×dX_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{a}\times d} be its design matrix. At iterate tt, the first-layer pre-activation on training observation ii is U~i,a(t)=Xi⊤​Wa,1(t)\widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(t)}=X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)} for i∈ℐai\in\mathcal{I}_{a}. To estimate test error from the training residuals, we account for observation ii’s influence on the gradient updates that produced Wa,1(t)W_{a,1}^{(t)}. The neural Onsager correction of Han and Imaizumi (2025) removes the leading self-interaction by adding a term to the hidden state. To define it, for each step rr, let

Ψi,a(r)≔(GWa,[2:L](r)(U~i,a(r))−Ri)∇uGWa,[2:L](r)(U~i,a(r))⊤∈ℝ1×q,\Psi_{i,a}^{(r)}\coloneqq\left(G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(r)}}(\widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(r)})-R_{i}\right)\nabla_{u}G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(r)}}(\widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(r)})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times q},

and let U~a(r)\widetilde{U}_{a}^{(r)} and Ψa(r)∈ℝNa×q\Psi_{a}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{a}\times q} collect the corresponding rows.

Thus, each row’s Ψi,a(r)\Psi_{i,a}^{(r)} is the gradient of (one half of) the squared residual with respect to the first-layer pre-activation, written as a row vector, so the first-layer loss gradient is Na−1​Xa⊤​Ψa(r)N_{a}^{-1}X_{a}^{\top}\Psi_{a}^{(r)}. From this training trajectory, the recursion detailed in Appendix B computes the Onsager matrices ρ^a,t,s∈ℝq×q\widehat{\rho}_{a,t,s}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}, s=1,…,ts=1,\ldots,t.

The GFOM-corrected hidden state is then defined as follows. We set U^i,a(0)=U~i,a(0)\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(0)}=\widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(0)} at initialization. At each subsequent iterate, the corrected hidden state for i∈ℐai\in\mathcal{I}_{a} is

U^i,a(t)=Xi⊤​Wa,1(t)+ϕa−1​∑s=1tηa,1(s−1)​Ψi,a(s−1)​ρ^a,t,s⊤∈ℝ1×q.\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)}=X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)}+\phi_{a}^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\eta_{a,1}^{(s-1)}\Psi_{i,a}^{(s-1)}\widehat{\rho}_{a,t,s}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times q}. (5)

Let U^a(t)∈ℝNa×q\widehat{U}_{a}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{a}\times q} collect these rows. It is computed from the same arm-wise training trajectory and does not require sample splitting, leave-one-out retraining, or knowledge of the true reward function.

3.2 Model Selection and Value Estimation without Sample Splitting

The corrected hidden states (5) are used to select the gradient-descent stopping iterate and estimate the target-policy value from the training sample only.

Model selection.

For each arm aa and each iterate t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, we define the corrected weighted residual criterion

ℰ^a(t)≔1Na∑i∈ℐawa(Xi)(Ri−GWa,[2:L](t)(U^i,a(t)))2.\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}w_{a}(X_{i})\left(R_{i}-G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}(\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)})\right)^{2}. (6)

The criterion replaces each fitted prediction in the importance-weighted average of squared training residuals with a prediction based on the corrected hidden state. Theorem 4.1 proves that it consistently estimates the fitted network’s weighted test risk, including the reward-noise contribution. We select the stopping iterate by minimizing this criterion:

t^a∈arg⁡mint∈𝒯⁡ℰ^a(t),\displaystyle\hat{t}_{a}\in\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}, (7)

breaking ties using a fixed ordering of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The selected iterate vector for the arms is therefore 𝐭^=(t^1,…,t^K)\hat{\mathbf{t}}=(\hat{t}_{1},\ldots,\hat{t}_{K}).

Value estimation.

Fix an iterate vector 𝐭∈𝒯K\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}. For observation ii, the model for action AiA_{i} was trained using that observation, so we evaluate it with the corrected hidden state. The models for the other actions were trained on disjoint observations, so we use their fitted predictions without correction. Define

g^𝐭(Xi,a)≔{GWa,[2:L](ta)(U^i,a(ta)),a=Ai,GWa,[2:L](ta)(Xi⊤Wa,1(ta)),a≠Ai.\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{t}}(X_{i},a)\coloneqq\begin{cases}G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t_{a})}}(\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t_{a})}),&a=A_{i},\\ G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t_{a})}}(X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t_{a})}),&a\neq A_{i}.\end{cases} (8)

The adjusted direct method (ADM) value estimator is

𝒱^ADM​(𝐭)≔1m​∑i=1m∑a=1Kν⁡(a|Xi)​g^𝐭​(Xi,a),\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})\coloneqq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X_{i})\,\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{t}}(X_{i},a), (9)

and the adjusted doubly robust (ADR) value estimator is

𝒱^ADR​(𝐭)≔𝒱^ADM​(𝐭)+1m​∑i=1mwAi​(Xi)​(Ri−g^𝐭​(Xi,Ai)).\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})\coloneqq\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})+\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})\left(R_{i}-\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{t}}(X_{i},A_{i})\right). (10)

The two procedures use the same corrected hidden states but target different quantities. The selection criterion estimates target-policy-weighted test risk. ADM estimates the fitted-model value, while ADR estimates the true policy value. Section 4 establishes consistency uniformly over the candidate iterations, without sample splitting. For a new context xx, we use the selected network g𝐭^​(x,a)g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}}(x,a); the adjustment in (8) is used only to evaluate observations included in that arm’s training sample.

4 Theoretical Guarantees

We first show that our in-sample selection criterion (6) uniformly estimates conditional arm-wise weighted test risk, enabling near-oracle early stopping (Section 4.1). We then establish consistency of ADM for the model-induced value and of ADR for the true policy value, contrast these guarantees with a one-step inconsistency example for uncorrected DR, and bound the conditional variance of a DR score evaluated on an independent observation (Section 4.2). Finally, we outline the proof strategy (Section 4.3). All results assume the statistical framework of Section 2 and the formal regularity conditions in Appendix C.

4.1 Consistent Risk Estimation and Near-Oracle Model Selection

For each arm aa, let Za∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)Z_{a}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and let ξanew\xi_{a}^{\mathrm{new}} have the law of εi|Ai=a\varepsilon_{i}\mid A_{i}=a. These draws are independent of each other and of the training sample and network initializations. The weighted test risk at iterate tt, conditional on the training data and initializations, is

ℰa,ind(t)≔𝔼⁡[wa​(Za)​(φa∗​(βa⊤​Za)+ξanew−fWa(t)​(Za))2|ℱtr],\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\!\left[w_{a}(Z_{a})\left(\varphi_{a}^{\ast}(\beta_{a}^{\top}Z_{a})+\xi_{a}^{\mathrm{new}}-f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z_{a})\right)^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}\right], (11)

where ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}} is generated by the training sample and all network initializations. The total test risk is ℛν​(g𝐭)=∑aμ⁡(a)​ℰa,ind(ta)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\mathbf{t}})=\sum_{a}\mu(a)\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t_{a})} almost surely. The following theorem shows that the criterion consistently estimates each arm’s conditional test risk, uniformly over t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}.

Theorem 4.1 (Uniform consistency).

Assume the statistical framework of Section 2 and the formal conditions in Appendix C. For every arm a∈[K]a\in[K], as Na,d→∞N_{a},d\to\infty with ϕa\phi_{a} bounded away from zero and infinity, the criterion in (6) and the conditional risk in (11) satisfy

supt∈𝒯|ℰ^a(t)−ℰa,ind(t)|→𝑝0.\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0.

This uniform consistency yields the following guarantee for the stopping rule t^a\hat{t}_{a} in (7). The proof is given in Appendix G.3.

Theorem 4.2 (Arm-wise iterate selection and oracle inequality).

Under the assumptions and asymptotic regime of Theorem 4.1, the selector in (7) satisfies, for every a∈[K]a\in[K],

ℰa,ind(t^a)≤mint∈𝒯⁡ℰa,ind(t)+op​(1).\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(\hat{t}_{a})}\leq\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}+o_{p}(1).

Moreover,

ℛν​(g𝐭^)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}) ≤min𝐭∈𝒯K⁡ℛν​(g𝐭)+op​(1),\displaystyle\leq\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\mathbf{t}})+o_{p}(1),
|𝒱g𝐭^​(ν)−𝒱⁡(ν)|2\displaystyle\left|\mathcal{V}_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right|^{2} ≤min𝐭∈𝒯K⁡ℛν∘​(g𝐭)+op​(1).\displaystyle\leq\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\mathbf{t}})+o_{p}(1).

The weighted test risk ℛν\mathcal{R}_{\nu} is the sum of the weighted prediction error ℛν∘\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ} and a noise term that does not depend on the fitted model. The bound on total test risk therefore also holds for ℛν∘\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}. Since ℛν∘​(g)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g) bounds |𝒱g​(ν)−𝒱⁡(ν)|2|\mathcal{V}_{g}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)|^{2}, as shown in Section 2.1, this gives the stated bound on the fitted model’s policy value error. Thus, without sample splitting, the selected models attain the smallest prediction risk among the candidate iterates up to op​(1)o_{p}(1).

4.2 Consistency of Value Estimation

ADM and ADR consistently estimate their respective values using the full training sample. A single gradient-descent step example first shows why the population identity Pd​ψg=𝒱⁡(ν)P_{d}\psi_{g}=\mathcal{V}(\nu) alone does not ensure consistency of uncorrected same-sample DR.

Inconsistency of DR evaluation on the training sample.

Consider the DR estimator formed by evaluating the fitted models directly on their training observations, 𝒱^DRnv​(𝐭)=m−1​∑iψg𝐭​(Qi)\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\mathbf{t})=m^{-1}\sum_{i}\psi_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(Q_{i}). Take ν=μ\nu=\mu and a constant reward R=cR=c almost surely. With Λ\Lambda as in Assumption C.1, fix 0<|c|≤Λ0<|c|\leq\Lambda and 0<η≤Λ0<\eta\leq\Lambda. For each arm, use a network with depth L=2L=2, width q=1q=1, and identity activation σ1=id\sigma_{1}=\mathrm{id}. Initialize Wa,1(0)=0W_{a,1}^{(0)}=0 and Wa,2(0)=1W_{a,2}^{(0)}=1, and set the first-layer learning rate to ηa,1(0)=η\eta_{a,1}^{(0)}=\eta.

For each observed arm, write X¯a=Na−1​∑i∈ℐaXi\overline{X}_{a}=N_{a}^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}X_{i}. The loss gradients at initialization are

∇Wa,1ℒa​(Wa(0))=−c​X¯a,∇Wa,2ℒa​(Wa(0))=0.\nabla_{W_{a,1}}\mathcal{L}_{a}(W_{a}^{(0)})=-c\,\overline{X}_{a},\qquad\nabla_{W_{a,2}}\mathcal{L}_{a}(W_{a}^{(0)})=0.

Thus, one simultaneous full-batch GD step produces

ga,1​(x)=η​c​x⊤​X¯a.g_{a,1}(x)=\eta c\,x^{\top}\overline{X}_{a}.

For i∈ℐai\in\mathcal{I}_{a}, the prediction ga,1​(Xi)g_{a,1}(X_{i}) contains the term η​c​‖Xi‖22/Na\eta c\|X_{i}\|_{2}^{2}/N_{a}, which is the contribution of observation ii to its own fitted prediction. This contribution does not vanish when NaN_{a} and dd grow proportionally. The following proposition yields the resulting policy-value error.

Proposition 4.3 (Inconsistency after one gradient-descent step).

For the constant-reward example in Section 4.2, assume the conditions of Theorem 4.1, 1∈𝒯1\in\mathcal{T}, and m/d→ϕ∈(0,∞)m/d\to\phi\in(0,\infty). Then

𝒱^DRnv​(1,…,1)−𝒱⁡(ν)→𝑝−η​c​(K−1)ϕ.\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(1,\ldots,1)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\xrightarrow{p}-\frac{\eta c(K-1)}{\phi}.

The limit is nonzero because c≠0c\neq 0, η>0\eta>0, and K≥2K\geq 2. Thus, the DR estimator is inconsistent at the fixed first GD iterate. Appendix H.1 gives the proof and also characterizes the error of 𝒱^DRnv\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}} uniformly over the candidate iterations, including choices made from the training data.

Consistency of ADM and ADR.

Correcting the training predictions yields the following guarantees for ADM (9) and ADR (10). ADM targets the population value induced by the learned reward model, while ADR targets the true policy value 𝒱⁡(ν)\mathcal{V}(\nu) (1). The proof is in Appendix H.

Theorem 4.4 (Uniform consistency of value estimation).

Under the assumptions and asymptotic regime of Theorem 4.1, the estimators in (9) and (10) satisfy

sup𝐭∈𝒯K|𝒱^ADM​(𝐭)−𝒱g𝐭​(ν)|→𝑝0,sup𝐭∈𝒯K|𝒱^ADR​(𝐭)−𝒱⁡(ν)|→𝑝0.\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(\nu)\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0,\qquad\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0.

Both conclusions hold for any choice 𝐭^∈𝒯K\widehat{\mathbf{t}}\in\mathcal{T}^{K} based on the training data and initializations, including the rule in (7). ADR remains consistent when the selected model’s prediction error does not converge to zero. ADM estimates the value induced by that model, so ADM minus ADR consistently estimates 𝒱g𝐭^​(ν)−𝒱​(ν)\mathcal{V}_{g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu), as formalized in Corollary H.2.

Variance of a DR score on an independent observation.

We now return to the role of prediction risk in controlling the variance of the score ψg​(X,A,R)\psi_{g}(X,A,R) in (3), evaluated on an observation independent of the training sample and initializations. Conditional on ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, the fitted model is fixed. Define the weighted prediction error

𝒥DR​(g)≔𝔼⁡[∑a=1Kν⁡(a∣X)​1−μ⁡(a)μ⁡(a)​{g⁡(X,a)−g∗​(X,a)}2|ℱtr].\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}}(g)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\mid X)\frac{1-\mu(a)}{\mu(a)}\{g(X,a)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\}^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}\right]. (12)

By the variance decomposition in Proposition H.10, 𝒥DR​(g)\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}}(g) bounds the increase in this conditional variance relative to the score using the true reward function g∗g^{\ast}. To state the consequence for model selection, define

c−​(μ)\displaystyle c_{-}(\mu) ≔mina∈[K]⁡1−μ⁡(a)μ⁡(a),\displaystyle\coloneqq\min_{a\in[K]}\frac{1-\mu(a)}{\mu(a)}, c+​(μ)\displaystyle c_{+}(\mu) ≔maxa∈[K]⁡1−μ⁡(a)μ⁡(a),\displaystyle\coloneqq\max_{a\in[K]}\frac{1-\mu(a)}{\mu(a)}, σeff2\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2} ≔Var⁡{ψg∗​(X,A,R)}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{g^{\ast}}(X,A,R)\}. (13)

Positivity and K≥2K\geq 2 imply 0<c−​(μ)≤c+​(μ)<∞0<c_{-}(\mu)\leq c_{+}(\mu)<\infty. By definition,

c−​(μ)​ℛν∘​(g)≤𝒥DR​(g)≤c+​(μ)​ℛν∘​(g).c_{-}(\mu)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g)\leq\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}}(g)\leq c_{+}(\mu)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g).

Applying Theorem 4.2 separately to each arm and weighting its regret by (1−μ⁡(a))/μ⁡(a)(1-\mu(a))/\mu(a) gives the following bound.

Corollary 4.5 (Conditional variance on an independent observation).

Under the assumptions and asymptotic regime of Theorem 4.2, let 𝐭^\hat{\mathbf{t}} be selected by (7). For an observation (X,A,R)(X,A,R) independent of ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, and with 𝒥DR\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}} and the constants defined in (12) and (13),

Var⁡{ψg𝐭^​(X,A,R)|ℱtr}≤σeff2+min𝐭∈𝒯K⁡𝒥DR​(g𝐭)+op​(1).\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(X,A,R)\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}\}\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}+\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}}(g_{\mathbf{t}})+o_{p}(1).

In particular, if min𝐭∈𝒯K⁡ℛν∘​(g𝐭)=op​(1)\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\mathbf{t}})=o_{p}(1), then

Var⁡{ψg𝐭^​(X,A,R)|ℱtr}=σeff2+op​(1).\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(X,A,R)\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}\}=\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}+o_{p}(1).

The proof is given in Appendix H.2. The corollary holds the selected model g𝐭^g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}} fixed and bounds the variance of its DR score (3) on a fresh observation. ADR in (10) averages corrected scores on the training sample. Its sampling variance also depends on covariances between these scores, which share fitted models and correction terms. Characterizing these joint fluctuations is left to future work.

We also note here that the cross-fitted value estimator requires a separate variance analysis in the proportional regime. Its standard m\sqrt{m}-convergence to Pm,d​ψg∗P_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}} argument uses vanishing fitted-score error, which is a much stronger condition under proportionally growing dd. In a related setting with linear outcomes and estimated logistic propensities, Jiang et al. (2025) characterize variance inflation and cross-fold covariance. This motivates our comparison of ADR both with cross-fitted DR and with the oracle DR benchmark empirically in Section 5.

4.3 Proof Strategy and Key Novelty

We outline the proof that the corrected criterion consistently estimates conditional test risk. The Onsager correction replaces U~i,a(t)\widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(t)} with U^i,a(t)\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)} (5) to account for observation ii’s contribution to its own fitted prediction; see Section 3.1.

State evolution approximates empirical averages along the training trajectory by expectations of functions of a jointly Gaussian sequence. Let 𝔘a(0)∈ℝq\mathfrak{U}_{a}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{q} represent the signal coordinate (βa⊤​Xi,0,…,0)(\beta_{a}^{\top}X_{i},0,\ldots,0), with zeros added to match the hidden-state dimension, and let 𝔘a(t+1)∈ℝq\mathfrak{U}_{a}^{(t+1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{q} be the Gaussian vector corresponding to the corrected hidden state at iterate tt. The unweighted theory of Han and Imaizumi (2025) compares averages of corrected fitted values and squared residuals with expectations under this state evolution.

A key technical challenge is the weighted risk in (6), which multiplies each squared residual by wa​(Xi)=ha​(Υ⊤​Xi)w_{a}(X_{i})=h_{a}(\Upsilon^{\top}X_{i}). Consequently, the analysis must track the policy index and learned hidden state jointly, since both depend on XiX_{i}.

We account for this dependence by appending a Gaussian vector 𝔘Υ,a∼𝒩⁡(0,Iℓ)\mathfrak{U}_{\Upsilon,a}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{\ell}) to the state evolution. The augmented recursion explicitly tracks its covariance with the learned hidden states:

Cov(𝔘a(s),𝔘Υ,a)=d−1/2Da,s−1⊤Υ,\operatorname{Cov}(\mathfrak{U}_{a}^{(s)},\mathfrak{U}_{\Upsilon,a})=d^{-1/2}D_{a,s-1}^{\top}\Upsilon,

where Da,s−1∈ℝd×qD_{a,s-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q} is the shift matrix defined by the arm-wise state-evolution recursion. The Gaussian law and covariance above are conditional on 𝒢a\mathcal{G}_{a}, which fixes the action labels, initialization, and realized noise. The recursion and conditioning are specified in Appendix C and Proposition S.2. The comparison is first established for the auxiliary GFOM and then transferred to the actual corrected states. For example, let Va(t)V_{a}^{(t)} denote the deeper-layer parameters in the state evolution. The weighted average of corrected predictions satisfies

1Na∑i∈ℐaha(Υ⊤Xi)GWa,[2:L](t)(U^i,a(t))=𝔼[ha(𝔘Υ,a)GVa(t)(𝔘a(t+1))∣𝒢a]+op(1).\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}h_{a}(\Upsilon^{\top}X_{i})G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}(\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[h_{a}(\mathfrak{U}_{\Upsilon,a})G_{V_{a}^{(t)}}(\mathfrak{U}_{a}^{(t+1)})\mid\mathcal{G}_{a}\right]+o_{p}(1).

An analogous comparison applies to the weighted squared residual, with the state-evolution expectation averaged over the realized noise values in arm aa. These comparisons hold uniformly over the fixed set of candidate iterations. They imply that ℰ^a(t)\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)} consistently estimates an intermediate test risk ℰa,π(t)\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)} that uses a new context and a noise value sampled uniformly from the realized training noises (Proposition E.3). Proposition F.2 then shows that replacing this empirical noise distribution with the true arm-specific noise law changes the risk by op​(1)o_{p}(1), uniformly over the candidate iterations. This yields consistency for the conditional test risk in (11).

The Onsager matrices are those of Han and Imaizumi (2025) since the target-policy weights enter evaluation, while training still minimizes the unweighted arm-wise squared loss.

5 Experiments

In this section, we examine whether the proposed criterion estimates the test risk of the full-data reward model, how its stopping decisions depend on the target policy, and how the correction affects value estimation. We also compare the value estimators’ mean squared errors at both fixed and increasing sample-to-dimension ratios. Experimental details are provided in Appendix J.

Risk estimation and early stopping.

We use a two-arm Gaussian bandit with uniform logging, nonlinear single-index rewards, and a context-dependent target policy. The reward models are sigmoid multilayer perceptrons trained by full-batch gradient descent. We increase d∈{128,256,512,1024,2048}d\in\{128,256,512,1024,2048\} with m=2​dm=2d, using 200 independent datasets per dimension. Appendix J specifies the data-generating model and training settings.

Figure 1 (left) compares risk estimates against the conditional test risk of the full-data model. Our corrected criterion’s root mean squared error (RMSE) decreases from 0.3470.347 to 0.0810.081, compared with 0.4100.410 to 0.1540.154 for ten-fold cross-validation (CV). At the largest dimension, correction nearly halves CV’s RMSE. Because CV evaluates models trained on fold complements, its discrepancy from full-data risk includes any difference between the test risks of the fold-complement and full-data models. Meanwhile, the importance-weighted mean squared training residuals remain inaccurate across all dimensions, with RMSE between 1.331.33 and 1.371.37.

Our corrected criterion also improves stopping decisions (Figure 1, right). We apply each rule’s selected iteration to the same full-data training trajectory. Selection regret is the excess total target-policy prediction risk ℛν∘\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ} over the best arm-wise stopping times on that trajectory. At d=2048d=2048, the corrected rule’s mean regret is 0.00250.0025, less than one-third of CV’s 0.00820.0082, while training-residual stopping has regret near 0.590.59. Appendix J.6 provides the risk curves and comparisons with networks retrained after omitting the evaluated observation.

The selection rule based on the corrected criterion and CV also achieve lower risk-estimation error and selection regret than single holdouts of sizes ⌈m⌉\lceil\sqrt{m}\rceil and ⌈m2/3⌉\lceil m^{2/3}\rceil at every tested dimension (Appendix J.3). These holdouts are faster; Appendix J.11 reports the computational comparison. Additional experiments with nonuniform logging or non-Gaussian contexts show decreasing corrected risk-estimation error and selection regret as dimension grows. ADR has lower absolute empirical bias than uncorrected DR in these settings (Appendices J.7 and J.8).

The role of target-policy weighting.

The stopping criterion should measure prediction error in the contexts where the target policy uses each arm. To isolate this dependence, we vary the target policy while holding the training data, network trajectories, and Onsager correction fixed. We use three arms and four target policies, with m=3​dm=3d at d∈{128,256,512}d\in\{128,256,512\}. Appendix J.4 specifies the reward links and policies.

Figure 2 compares the corrected weighted criterion with unweighted selection and target-weighted ten-fold CV. Averaging over the three nonuniform policies at each dimension, weighting reduces the selected model’s prediction risk by 0.0310.031–0.0330.033 relative to unweighted selection. For the uniform policy, the weighted and unweighted rules coincide.

Relative to target-weighted CV, the corrected weighted rule reduces prediction risk by 0.0270.027–0.0290.029, again averaging over the three nonuniform policies at each dimension. Its mean selection regret is lower than CV’s for every policy and dimension. Appendix J.4 reports the paired comparisons.

Value estimation at the same fitted model.

We next isolate the effect of the value correction. Returning to the two-arm experiment with m=2​dm=2d, we select the reward model using the corrected criterion and compute DR and ADR from the same fitted networks, stopping times, and logged observations. Figure 3 (left) shows that correction reduces the persistent bias of same-sample DR. At d=2048d=2048, the empirical bias magnitude falls by over 95%95\%, from 0.01490.0149 for DR to 0.00060.0006 for ADR.

To compare precision for the fitted-model value, we also evaluate DM and ADM against the population value induced by their shared fitted model, 𝒱g𝐭^​(ν)\mathcal{V}_{g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu), computed separately for each dataset. This is the target of the ADM guarantee in Theorem 4.4. Cross-arm DM provides an independent-evaluation comparison: it evaluates each selected arm model on contexts logged under the other arm, avoiding reuse of its training observations. ADM reduces MSE relative to cross-arm DM by 50.7%50.7\%–57.4%57.4\% across the five dimensions, with every paired 95%95\% interval favoring ADM (Figure 3, right; Appendix J.2).

Comparison with cross-fitted DR.

The corrected criterion also improves model selection within ten-fold cross-fitted DR (CF10). Our inner-validation CF10 baseline selects the stopping time on an inner split before refitting on the complete training complement. Selecting directly on that complement with the corrected criterion avoids this additional training-size mismatch while keeping the evaluation fold excluded from fitting and selection. Corrected stopping reduces the complement models’ prediction error by 19.3%19.3\%–42.3%42.3\% relative to inner validation (Appendix J.5). We compare both CF10 procedures with ADR, which trains and selects on all available observations for each arm.

Figure 4 shows that ADR has similar observed MSE to corrected-stopping CF10, with substantially lower runtime (Appendix J.11). At d=2048d=2048, their RMSEs are 0.01830.0183 and 0.01850.0185, respectively. ADR has lower MSE point estimates at every dimension, with most paired 95%95\% intervals including zero. At d=2048d=2048, ADR also has lower MSE than IPS and self-normalized IPS (SNIPS), with paired 95%95\% intervals favoring ADR. Appendix J.5 reports the paired comparisons and bias–variance decomposition.

Value estimation under increasing sample-to-dimension ratio.

We next examine how the value estimation precision comparison changes as sample size outgrows dimension, using the oracle DR benchmark introduced in Section 4.2. Finally, we examine value estimation as m/dm/d increases, both at fixed d=256d=256 and while dimension grows. Figure 5 reports MSE normalized by σeff2/m\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}/m, the MSE of DR using the true reward function. At the largest sample sizes, ADR and both CF10 procedures have similar MSEs near this oracle benchmark. At (d,m)=(1024,32768)(d,m)=(1024,32768), the estimated normalized MSEs of ADR and corrected-stopping CF10 are 1.0001.000 and 1.0131.013, respectively. ADR also has lower MSE than IPS and SNIPS at both endpoints with m=32768m=32768. Appendix J.10 gives the implementation details and paired comparisons.

Across the tested regimes, ADR achieves precision comparable to corrected-stopping CF10, with substantially lower runtime in the matched benchmarks (Appendix J.11).

We report the wall-clock runtime for complete ADR, cross-validation, and cross-fitting procedures, including model selection and refitting where required in Appendix J.11.

6 Discussion

We study how to select a reward model trained on the full logged sample and estimate policy value using the same observations. In the proportional regime, our Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion consistently estimates conditional test risk and yields near-oracle stopping among the candidate gradient descent iterates. The correction also enables consistent estimation of the fitted-model value through ADM (9) and the true policy value through ADR (10), without requiring reward prediction error to vanish.

The experiments in Section 5 demonstrate benefits for both full-sample learning and cross-fitting. The corrected criterion improves full-data stopping selection over cross validation and two holdout sample schedules. For estimating the policy value induced by the fitted model, ADM achieves lower RMSE than both (uncorrected) DM on the full sample and cross-arm evaluation. For doubly robust value estimation with 10-fold cross-fitting (CF10), our Onsager-corrected criterion selects directly on each complete training complement and yields reward models with lower mean target-policy-weighted prediction risk than standard inner validation followed by refitting. Full-data ADR achieves comparable observed RMSE to corrected-stopping CF10 at substantially lower runtime.

Note that our experiments (Figure 5) show that ADR and CF10 attain similar MSEs near the oracle DR benchmark as sample size outgrows dimension. These findings motivate for future work a fluctuation theory for ADR that accounts for dependence between its Onsager-corrected scores, as discussed in Section 4.2. Two goals remain: to derive a central limit theorem (CLT) for ADR in the proportional regime and to identify conditions for recovering the same limit as the oracle DR estimator, when d→∞d\to\infty with d/m→0d/m\to 0. For example, showing that ADR differs from Pm,d​ψg∗P_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}} by op(m−1/2)o_{p}(m^{-1/2}) would give ADR the same limiting distribution whenever the oracle estimator satisfies a CLT.

Finally, our analysis assumes Gaussian contexts and known context-independent logging. Promising results on experiments with non-Gaussian designs (see Appendix J.8) motivate extending our weighted state-evolution analysis beyond Gaussian designs. An important next step is also to extend our analysis to context-dependent logging: since it changes the distribution of contexts within each arm’s training sample, it requires a new characterization of the resulting training dynamics and correction.

Appendix

After related work, Appendices B and C give the computable Onsager recursion and formal assumptions. The proof has five steps. First, we condition on the logged actions to obtain an arm-wise regression problem (Proposition S.1). Second, we append the target-policy index to the state evolution (Proposition S.2). Third, we compare corrected training averages with independent-context expectations (Proposition S.3). Fourth, we replace resampled training noise with independent test noise (Proposition F.2). Finally, a finite union over the iterate grid yields the selection and ADM/ADR consistency results (Appendices G and H). Appendix I provides rates under a stronger envelope-moment condition. Appendix H.1 characterizes uncorrected same-sample DR error and its connection to classical empirical-process conditions for first-order inference.

Appendix A Related Work

Reward models in off-policy evaluation.

Classic OPE baselines include the direct method (DM) [Beygelzimer and Langford, 2009], inverse propensity scoring (IPS) [Precup et al., 2000, Strehl et al., 2010], and doubly robust (DR) estimators [Dudík et al., 2011, Dudík et al., 2014]. Subsequent work improves the value estimator’s bias–variance tradeoff through sample-wise interpolation between DR and DM (SWITCH [Wang et al., 2017]), variance-targeted reward modeling (MRDR [Farajtabar et al., 2018]), adaptive blending (CAB [Su et al., 2019]), and smooth importance-weight corrections (DRos [Su et al., 2020a] and IPS-λ\lambda/DR-λ\lambda [Metelli et al., 2021]). Our criterion estimates the target-policy-weighted test risk of a neural reward model fitted on the full sample. The corresponding prediction error bounds the squared difference between the model-induced and true policy values, and the additional variance of a DR score evaluated on independent observations.

Semiparametric estimation and sample reuse.

The same-sample empirical-process term in (4) is standard in semiparametric analysis [Kennedy, 2024]. When the data distribution is fixed, stochastic equicontinuity of a Donsker empirical process and L2L^{2} convergence of the fitted score to the score using the true reward function make this term op​(1)o_{p}(1). Cross-fitting uses independent evaluation observations for each nuisance fit [Schick, 1986, Chernozhukov et al., 2018]; own-observation effects and cross-fitting also appear in series-based semiparametric estimation [Newey and Robins, 2018]. Stability conditions permit inference without splitting for suitable learners [Chen et al., 2022]. Our correction establishes risk and value consistency along a neural training trajectory in proportional dimension. In this regime, Jiang et al. [2025] find variance inflation and non-negligible cross-fold covariance for cross-fitted DR with linear outcomes and logistic propensities. These findings motivate future work in studying ADR’s limiting distribution and asymptotic variance, the analysis of which must account for dependence among its corrected scores.

Value estimator selection and reward-model selection.

Several OPE methods select the value estimator or its hyperparameters. SLOPE [Su et al., 2020b, Tucker and Lee, 2021] tunes parameters that control the value estimator’s bias–variance tradeoff, while PAS-IF [Udagawa et al., 2023] selects value estimators using pseudo-evaluation policies. Cross-validated OPE also selects value estimators and their hyperparameters [Cief et al., 2025]. McGrath et al. [2026] study ridge-based estimation of expected conditional covariance under proportional asymptotics. Prediction-optimal nuisance tuning need not minimize the estimator’s asymptotic variance. Our selector targets weighted test risk; the corresponding prediction risk bounds the additional variance under independent DR evaluation. A held-out importance-weighted residual criterion estimates weighted test risk for a model trained on the complementary sample [Sugiyama et al., 2007]. Cross-validation followed by full-data refitting is therefore a natural comparison for our stopping rule.

Cross-fitting likewise uses models trained on fewer observations than the full-data fit. Within each fold’s training sample, one may use a further validation split to select a stopping iterate and then refit on that training sample. The validation criterion then estimates the risk of the models before refitting, while DR evaluation on the excluded fold uses the refitted model. Our Onsager-corrected criterion can select directly on the complete training complement, while the excluded fold remains independent for DR evaluation; Appendix J.5 examines this use.

Reward modeling and neural state evolution.

Single-index reward models have been studied for online regret minimization through kernel regression, cross-fitting, and staged exploration [Kang et al., 2026, Ma and Cai, 2025, Arya et al., 2026]. Our setting concerns offline evaluation and selection of neural reward models in proportional dimension. Related work constructs risk estimates along gradient-descent trajectories for high-dimensional linear and robust regression [Bellec and Tan, 2026, Tan and Bellec, 2024] and develops inference for empirical risk minimization [Han and Xu, 2024]. We build directly on Han and Imaizumi [2025], who establish state evolution for finite-width neural networks, a computable Onsager correction, consistent estimation of unweighted test error, and early stopping based on that estimate. We retain their correction for the unweighted arm-wise training loss and extend the joint state evolution to include the linear projections that determine the target-policy probabilities. Tracking the covariance between these projections and the learned features gives the weighted risk-estimation and OPE results proved here.

Its coefficients are q×qq\times q matrices ρ^a,t,s\widehat{\rho}_{a,t,s}, s=1,…,ts=1,\ldots,t, computed from the same training trajectory by the recursion of Han and Imaizumi [2025]. We give that recursion below. For observation i∈ℐai\in\mathcal{I}_{a} and step rr, write its loss as a function of the hidden state:

=(Qa,k[t−1]0−ba,k[t]​Qa,k[t−1]ηa,1(t−1)​Jia,k,a(t−1)).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}Q_{a,k}^{[t-1]}&0\\ -b_{a,k}^{[t]}Q_{a,k}^{[t-1]}&\eta_{a,1}^{(t-1)}J_{i_{a,k},a}^{(t-1)}\end{pmatrix}.

In particular, the leading blocks of Qa,k[t]Q_{a,k}^{[t]} and 𝝉^a[t]\widehat{\bm{\tau}}_{a}^{[t]} agree with their preceding values. The leading block of 𝝆^a[t]\widehat{\bm{\rho}}_{a}^{[t]} is consequently

It−1,q+(𝝉^a[t−1]+It−1,q)​𝔒t−1​(𝝆^a[t−2])=𝝆^a[t−1],I_{t-1,q}+(\widehat{\bm{\tau}}_{a}^{[t-1]}+I_{t-1,q})\mathfrak{O}_{t-1}(\widehat{\bm{\rho}}_{a}^{[t-2]})=\widehat{\bm{\rho}}_{a}^{[t-1]},

which completes the induction. Thus, the system Ba,k[t]​Qa,k[t]=𝑳^a,k[t−1]B_{a,k}^{[t]}Q_{a,k}^{[t]}=\widehat{\bm{L}}_{a,k}^{[t-1]} can be solved by updating only the new block row. This is block forward substitution using the cached solution, and requires no dense inverse.

Algorithm 2 summarizes the resulting post-processing computation.

Implementation and complexity.

The algorithm reuses the leading solution and Onsager blocks from the preceding iteration. Computing the new block rows at iteration tt costs O⁡(Na​q3​t2)O(N_{a}q^{3}t^{2}) operations for one arm, and all TT iterations cost

∑t=1TO⁡(Na​q3​t2)=O⁡(Na​q3​T3).\sum_{t=1}^{T}O(N_{a}q^{3}t^{2})=O(N_{a}q^{3}T^{3}).

At the final iteration, each row cache has T2T^{2} blocks of size q×qq\times q, so the block cache stores O⁡(Na​T2​q2)O(N_{a}T^{2}q^{2}) numbers. Computing the local derivatives adds O⁡(Na​L​q3​T)O(N_{a}Lq^{3}T) operations. For fixed LL, this cost remains within the correction bound. These costs are additional to full-batch training, whose first-layer operations cost O⁡(Na​d​q​T)O(N_{a}dqT). End-to-end storage includes O⁡(Na​d)O(N_{a}d) for the design and O⁡(d​q​T)O(dqT) for the first-layer parameter trajectory, in addition to the correction cache and lower-order fixed-width arrays. Thus, when d≍Nad\asymp N_{a} and K,L,q,TK,L,q,T are fixed, the correction preserves the leading asymptotic dependence on sample size. Its finite-sample overhead can be substantial.

Appendix C Notation and Formal Assumptions for the Working Regime

The working regime uses the i.i.d. observations of Section 2, with Gaussian contexts, single-index conditional reward means, known context-independent logging under positivity, and a target policy specified independently of the logged sample with the stated multi-index importance weights. We take m/d→ϕ∈(0,∞)m/d\to\phi\in(0,\infty), with K,L,q,ℓK,L,q,\ell fixed and 𝒯⊂ℤ≥0\mathcal{T}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} finite, nonempty, and fixed. The noise and initialization conditions used in the proofs are specified below.

They may depend on the fixed iteration tt, moment order rr, and fixed model and regularity parameters, and their values may change from line to line. When rr is fixed, we suppress it and write Ct,ctC_{t},c_{t}. We set maxima over empty index sets equal to zero. Unsubscripted vector norms are Euclidean and unsubscripted matrix norms are Frobenius; ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty} denotes the largest absolute entry and ∥⋅∥op\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}} the spectral norm. For a nonnegative random quantity YdY_{d}, the notation Yd=dop​(1)Y_{d}=d^{o_{p}(1)} denotes a subpolynomial upper bound: d−ϵ​Yd→𝑝0d^{-\epsilon}Y_{d}\xrightarrow{p}0 for every fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0. For integers r≤sr\leq s, write [r:s]={r,r+1,…,s}[r:s]=\{r,r+1,\ldots,s\} and [n]=[1:n][n]=[1:n]. We write z([r:s])=(z(r),…,z(s))z^{([r:s])}=(z^{(r)},\ldots,z^{(s)}). Thus, ℝq[r:s]\mathbb{R}^{q[r:s]} denotes the product of s−r+1s-r+1 copies of ℝq\mathbb{R}^{q}. We write Mk⋅M_{k\cdot} and M⋅jM_{\cdot j} for a matrix’s kkth row and jjth column. When forming augmented matrices, (U,V)(U,V) denotes column concatenation of matrices with the same number of rows. For a real-valued function ff, its Lipschitz seminorm is ‖f‖Lip=supx≠y|f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)|/‖x−y‖\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}=\sup_{x\neq y}|f(x)-f(y)|/\|x-y\|. A function f:ℝn→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is Λf\Lambda_{f}-pseudo-Lipschitz of order p≥1p\geq 1 if

|f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)|≤Λf​(1+‖x‖+‖y‖)p−1​‖x−y‖for all ​x,y∈ℝn.|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\Lambda_{f}(1+\|x\|+\|y\|)^{p-1}\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Since the logging policy is context-independent, the sample decomposes arm-wise. ‖Dj​𝝋​(w)‖\displaystyle\|D^{j}\bm{\varphi}(w)\| ≤Cq​Λ​(1+‖w‖)r0,\displaystyle\leq C_{q}\Lambda(1+\|w\|)^{r_{0}}, j=0,1,2,3,\displaystyle j=0,1,2,3,

To make the derivative bounds explicit, let 𝒢V​(u)\mathscr{G}_{V}(u) denote the network output as a function of its first-layer hidden state, with the deeper weights VV fixed. In column-vector notation its loss gradient is

×(‖u−u′‖+‖w−w′‖+‖V−V′‖).\displaystyle\qquad\times(\|u-u^{\prime}\|+\|w-w^{\prime}\|+\|V-V^{\prime}\|).

Here the derivatives DjD^{j} are with respect to (u,w)(u,w), and the second bound follows by the product rule and integration along the segment joining the two arguments, including their deeper weights. In particular, a change in D​𝝋​(w)D\bm{\varphi}(w) is controlled by ‖w−w′‖\|w-w^{\prime}\|.

Each auxiliary output row depends only on the corresponding input rows. The generic GFOM theorems allow these maps to vary across rows and coordinates. Lemma S.1.2 applies these theorems to smooth input cutoffs and removes the cutoffs using polynomial moment bounds. The deterministic gradient-descent comparison uses the loss gradient identity and the value bounds above. For the Onsager comparison, the finite polynomial expansion of the block inverse is controlled by the sum of the two state envelopes, as verified in Lemma S.1.3. These arguments preserve every other hypothesis and give the stated componentwise-link conclusions.

Corollary C.3 (Arbitrary fixed index directions under Gaussian design).

Assume the working conditions above, except for the coordinate bounds on βa\beta_{a} and γj\gamma_{j} and the envelope condition (18). Then, the conclusions of Theorems 4.1, 4.2 and 4.4 hold for arbitrary fixed orientations of the reward and policy-index directions.

Condition on 𝒲(0)\mathcal{W}^{(0)} and let

S=span{βa,γj,(Wa,1(0))⋅k:a∈[K],j∈[ℓ],k∈[q]},r=dimS≤K+ℓ+Kq.S=\operatorname{span}\{\beta_{a},\gamma_{j},(W_{a,1}^{(0)})_{\cdot k}:a\in[K],j\in[\ell],k\in[q]\},\qquad r=\dim S\leq K+\ell+Kq.

Choose an orthonormal basis B∈ℝd×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} of SS measurably in 𝒲(0)\mathcal{W}^{(0)}, for example by Gram–Schmidt applied in a fixed order and omitting dependent columns. For v∈Sv\in S,

d​‖Q⊤​v‖∞=d​‖C​B⊤​v‖∞≤2​‖B⊤​v‖1≤2​r​‖v‖.\sqrt{d}\,\|Q^{\top}v\|_{\infty}=\sqrt{d}\,\|CB^{\top}v\|_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{2}\,\|B^{\top}v\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{2r}\,\|v\|.

Apply this rotation jointly to the contexts and first-layer parameters:

Xi′=Q⊤Xi,βa′=Q⊤βa,Υ′=Q⊤Υ,Wa,1′(0)=Q⊤Wa,1(0).X_{i}^{\prime}=Q^{\top}X_{i},\qquad\beta_{a}^{\prime}=Q^{\top}\beta_{a},\qquad\Upsilon^{\prime}=Q^{\top}\Upsilon,\qquad W_{a,1}^{\prime}{}^{(0)}=Q^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(0)}.

Leave actions, rewards, noise, and deeper-layer initializations unchanged. Conditional on 𝒲(0)\mathcal{W}^{(0)}, the rotated contexts remain i.i.d. N⁡(0,Id)N(0,I_{d}), independent of the actions and arm-specific noises. The signal and policy directions satisfy their required coordinate bounds with constant 2​(K+ℓ+K​q)\sqrt{2(K+\ell+Kq)}. For each initial first-layer column,

‖(Wa,1(0))⋅k‖≤‖d​Wa,1(0)‖∞.\|(W_{a,1}^{(0)})_{\cdot k}\|\leq\|\sqrt{d}\,W_{a,1}^{(0)}\|_{\infty}.

Consequently the rotated envelope satisfies maxa⁡ϰ∗,a′≤C0​κ0,d=dop​(1)\max_{a}\varkappa_{\ast,a}^{\prime}\leq C_{0}\kappa_{0,d}=d^{o_{p}(1)} for a constant C0C_{0} depending only on K,ℓ,qK,\ell,q.

The conditional comparison arguments apply with all original initializations retained in the conditioning fields. In particular, condition on 𝒲(0)\mathcal{W}^{(0)}, the action labels, and the noises in an arm. The rotated directions and parameters are then fixed, and that arm’s context rows are still independent standard Gaussians. The bounds in Lemmas E.1 and S.2 are uniform in these fixed directions and initializations once their coordinate bounds and envelope are specified. Their error bounds are polynomial in ϰ∗,a′​log⁡d\varkappa_{\ast,a}^{\prime}\log d times a negative power of dd, so they vanish in probability under (21). Conditional probability bounds may be truncated at one before averaging over the initialization and noise. The empirical noise moments are unchanged by rotation. Conditioning additionally on all initializations also preserves the independence used when predictions are evaluated on another arm’s observations. Thus, the risk and value consistency proofs apply to the rotated system, as does the finite-grid selection argument.

It remains to identify their conclusions with the original quantities. Induction in the simultaneous gradient updates gives

Wa,1′=(t)Q⊤Wa,1(t),Wa,α′=(t)Wa,α(t)(α≥2).W_{a,1}^{\prime}{}^{(t)}=Q^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)},\qquad W_{a,\alpha}^{\prime}{}^{(t)}=W_{a,\alpha}^{(t)}\quad(\alpha\geq 2).

Indeed, Xi′⊤Wa,1′(t)=Xi⊤Wa,1(t)X_{i}^{\prime}{}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{\prime}{}^{(t)}=X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)}, so hidden states and deeper-layer gradients agree, and the first-layer gradient is multiplied by Q⊤Q^{\top}. The signal and policy indices, hidden-state Hessians, estimated Onsager coefficients, and corrected predictions therefore agree. Hence, the criteria, selected iterations under the same tie rule, and value estimators agree pathwise.

Keep the original initialization in the rotated training field:

σ⁡(𝒲(0),(Xi′,Ai,Ri)i∈[m])=σ⁡(𝒲(0),𝒟m)=ℱtr.\sigma(\mathcal{W}^{(0)},(X_{i}^{\prime},A_{i},R_{i})_{i\in[m]})=\sigma(\mathcal{W}^{(0)},\mathcal{D}_{m})=\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}.

This equality holds because QQ is measurable in the retained initialization and the transformation of contexts is invertible given it; it does not require recovering the original initialization from its rotated weights. For a new Gaussian context ZZ independent of ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, let Z′=Q⊤​ZZ^{\prime}=Q^{\top}Z. Its conditional law is still N⁡(0,Id)N(0,I_{d}), and predictions, policy weights, and reward means agree at the coupled contexts. Conditional test risks and fitted-model values are therefore equal. This proves the stated conclusions. ∎

Appendix D From Logged Data to Arm-wise State Evolution

This section reduces the logged bandit data to the setting of Han and Imaizumi [2025]. Conditional on the action labels and counts, each arm gives a Gaussian single-index regression problem with its own initialization and noise vector. We then append the target-policy index to the auxiliary GFOM iterates. This allows the state-evolution test functions to include the importance weights.

Lemma D.1 (Fresh-draw conditioning).

Let Θa\Theta_{a} be ℱ^a\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}-measurable, and let QQ be independent of ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. If ℱ^a⊆ℋ⊆ℱtr\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}\subseteq\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, then every nonnegative measurable function bb satisfies

𝔼⁡[b⁡(Q,Θa)|ℋ]=∫b⁡(q,Θa)​d​PQ​(q)almost surely.\mathbb{E}[b(Q,\Theta_{a})\,|\,\mathcal{H}]=\int b(q,\Theta_{a})\,dP_{Q}(q)\qquad\text{almost surely}.

The identity also holds for signed bb when ∫|b⁡(q,Θa)|​d​PQ​(q)<∞\int|b(q,\Theta_{a})|\,dP_{Q}(q)<\infty almost surely, with conditional expectations interpreted by this finite fresh-draw integral.

Proof.

The variable Θa\Theta_{a} is ℋ\mathcal{H}-measurable, and the conditional law of QQ given ℋ\mathcal{H} is its marginal law. The identity follows first for bounded bb and then for nonnegative bb by monotone convergence. For signed bb, apply the nonnegative identity to its positive and negative parts; the assumed absolute-integral bound makes both terms finite. ∎

In particular, the lemma applies with ℋ\mathcal{H} equal to ℱ^a\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}, σ⁡(𝒟m,Wa(0))\sigma(\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}), or ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. These conditioning fields therefore give the same expectation for a fixed arm-wise predictor evaluated at a fresh draw.

We next establish the bounds needed for the state-evolution and Onsager comparisons. We first control the gradient-descent iterates, then prove an averaged comparison for the auxiliary GFOM, and finally compare the two recursions and their Onsager coefficients before returning to the appended policy index.

Lemma S.1.1 (Bounds for gradient-descent iterates).

Assume the working conditions of Appendix C. Fix an arm on EcntE_{\mathrm{cnt}}, condition on 𝒢a\mathcal{G}_{a}, and write m=Nam=N_{a}, n=dn=d, ϕ=m/n\phi=m/n, and κ=ϰ∗,a\kappa=\varkappa_{\ast,a}. Suppress the arm subscript, and fix a horizon T≥1T\geq 1. For every b0>0b_{0}>0, there is Cb0<∞C_{b_{0}}<\infty such that

ℙ{max0≤s≤T∥XW1(s)∥∞>(Cb0κlogn)Cb0|𝒢a}≤(Cb0κlogn)Cb0n−b0.\mathbb{P}\left\{\max_{0\leq s\leq T}\|XW_{1}^{(s)}\|_{\infty}>(C_{b_{0}}\kappa\log n)^{C_{b_{0}}}\mathrel{\big|}\mathcal{G}_{a}\right\}\leq(C_{b_{0}}\kappa\log n)^{C_{b_{0}}}n^{-b_{0}}. (22)

For every fixed r≥1r\geq 1, there is Cr<∞C_{r}<\infty such that

𝔼[{1+max0≤s≤T(∥XW1(s)∥∞+∥W1(s)∥+max2≤α≤L∥Wα(s)∥)}r|𝒢a]≤(Crκlogn)Cr.\mathbb{E}\left[\left\{1+\max_{0\leq s\leq T}\left(\|XW_{1}^{(s)}\|_{\infty}+\|W_{1}^{(s)}\|+\max_{2\leq\alpha\leq L}\|W_{\alpha}^{(s)}\|\right)\right\}^{r}\mathrel{\big|}\mathcal{G}_{a}\right]\leq(C_{r}\kappa\log n)^{C_{r}}. (23)

The constants are uniform in m,n,κm,n,\kappa on EcntE_{\mathrm{cnt}}.

All probabilities and expectations in this proof are conditional on 𝒢a\mathcal{G}_{a}. Exponents denoted by CTC_{T} depend only on the fixed horizon and regularity parameters, independently of the tail exponent bb; multiplicative constants denoted by CbC_{b} may depend on bb. We take n≥3n\geq 3; changing the constants covers smaller nn. Set A=X/nA=X/\sqrt{n} and w=X​β[q]w=X\beta_{[q]}. The definition of κ\kappa bounds n​‖β‖∞\sqrt{n}\|\beta\|_{\infty}, n​‖W1(0)‖∞\sqrt{n}\|W_{1}^{(0)}\|_{\infty}, the initial deeper weights, and ‖ξ‖∞\|\xi\|_{\infty}. In particular, ‖β‖+‖W1(0)‖≤C​κ\|\beta\|+\|W_{1}^{(0)}\|\leq C\kappa. Gaussian spectral-norm and coordinate-tail bounds imply, for each b>0b>0,

ℙ⁡(𝒜bc)≤Cb​n−b,𝒜b={‖A‖op≤Cb,‖w‖∞≤Cb​κ​log⁡n}.\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{A}_{b}^{c})\leq C_{b}n^{-b},\qquad\mathcal{A}_{b}=\{\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C_{b},\ \|w\|_{\infty}\leq C_{b}\kappa\sqrt{\log n}\}.

Also every fixed moment of Q=1+‖A‖op+κ+‖w‖∞Q=1+\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\kappa+\|w\|_{\infty} is bounded by (C​κ​log⁡n)C(C\kappa\log n)^{C}.

We first control the weights without using a bound on individual hidden states. Let 𝒢V​(u)\mathscr{G}_{V}(u) denote the network output when the first-layer pre-activation is uu and the deeper weights are VV. The bounded activation derivatives imply

‖DVα​𝒢V​(u)‖\displaystyle\|D_{V_{\alpha}}\mathscr{G}_{V}(u)\| ≤C​(1+‖V‖)C​(1+‖u‖).\displaystyle\leq C(1+\|V\|)^{C}(1+\|u\|). (24)

Here and below any fixed norm on the finite collection of deeper weights may be used. For v=n​W1v=\sqrt{n}W_{1} and u=A​vu=Av, the first-layer update is

v+=v−ϕ−1​η1​A⊤​𝔖​(u,w,V).v^{+}=v-\phi^{-1}\eta_{1}A^{\top}\mathfrak{S}(u,w,V).

supmaxs⁡‖B(s)‖≤Rℙ{max1≤s≤T+1∥uB(s)∥∞>(CbκRlogn)CT}≤Cbn−b.\sup_{\max_{s}\|B^{(s)}\|\leq R}\mathbb{P}\left\{\max_{1\leq s\leq T+1}\|u_{B}^{(s)}\|_{\infty}>(C_{b}\kappa R\log n)^{C_{T}}\right\}\leq C_{b}n^{-b}. (27)

sup‖B‖≤Rmaxs≤Tn−1/2∥vB(s)∥≤(CbκRlogn)CT.\sup_{\|B\|\leq R}\max_{s\leq T}n^{-1/2}\|v_{B}^{(s)}\|\leq(C_{b}\kappa R\log n)^{C_{T}}.

maxs≤T+1⁡‖uB(s)−uB′(s)‖∞≤(Cb​n​κ​R​log⁡n)CT​‖B−B′‖.\max_{s\leq T+1}\|u_{B}^{(s)}-u_{B^{\prime}}^{(s)}\|_{\infty}\leq(C_{b}n\kappa R\log n)^{C_{T}}\|B-B^{\prime}\|. (28)

The next lemma compares empirical averages of the auxiliary row and column histories with their state-evolution expectations. {(uk(s),Xk⋅Υ)}s=0T,{(Θk(s)(𝔘([0:s])),𝔘Υ)}s=0T,\{(u_{k}^{(s)},X_{k\cdot}\Upsilon)\}_{s=0}^{T},\qquad\{(\Theta_{k}^{(s)}(\mathfrak{U}^{([0:s])}),\mathfrak{U}_{\Upsilon})\}_{s=0}^{T},

Proof.

All expectations and probabilities below are conditional on 𝒢a\mathcal{G}_{a}. Constants may depend on the fixed horizon, moment orders, depth, width, growth order, and the constants in Appendix C. They are independent of nn, κ\kappa, and the cutoff radius introduced below. We use the original deterministic sequences V(s)V^{(s)} and M(s)M^{(s)} throughout the construction.

Choose a smooth function χ:ℝ→ℝ\chi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} equal to the identity on [−1,1][-1,1] and constant outside [−2,2][-2,2], with |χ⁡(x)|≤C​|x||\chi(x)|\leq C|x|. For R≥1R\geq 1, set χR​(x)=R​χ​(x/R)\chi_{R}(x)=R\chi(x/R) and apply it coordinatewise. Replace the row loss gradient in Gs⟨2⟩G_{s}^{\langle 2\rangle} by

𝔖ˇs,k,R​(u,w)=𝔖k​(χR​(u),χR​(w),V(s−1)),1≤s≤T.\check{\mathfrak{S}}_{s,k,R}(u,w)=\mathfrak{S}_{k}\bigl(\chi_{R}(u),\chi_{R}(w),V^{(s-1)}\bigr),\qquad 1\leq s\leq T. (29)

All other auxiliary maps, including Fs⟨2⟩F_{s}^{\langle 2\rangle} and its original M(s−1)M^{(s-1)}, are unchanged. The appended maps remain constant or zero. Check marks refer to this construction. In particular, vˇα(s)=vα(s)=Vα(s)\check{v}_{\alpha}^{(s)}=v_{\alpha}^{(s)}=V_{\alpha}^{(s)} for α≥2\alpha\geq 2: the corresponding columns of AA vanish, and the deterministic update is Vα(s−1)−ηα(s−1)​Mα(s−1)V_{\alpha}^{(s-1)}-\eta_{\alpha}^{(s-1)}M_{\alpha}^{(s-1)}.

We first record bounds that do not grow with RR. Let 𝒢V​(u)\mathscr{G}_{V}(u) be the qq-dimensional network output as a function of its first-layer hidden state. In the derivative calculations below, regard the row states and loss gradients as column vectors. The loss gradient is

𝔖k​(u,w,V)=D​𝒢V​(u)⊤​{𝒢V​(u)−𝝋⁡(w)−ξk​e1}.\mathfrak{S}_{k}(u,w;V)=D\mathscr{G}_{V}(u)^{\top}\{\mathscr{G}_{V}(u)-\bm{\varphi}(w)-\xi_{k}e_{1}\}.

The activation and link assumptions, the product rule, and the chain rule give, for j=0,1,2,3j=0,1,2,3,

‖Dj​𝔖k​(u,w,V)‖≤C​(1+‖V‖+|ξk|+‖u‖+‖w‖)C.\|D^{j}\mathfrak{S}_{k}(u,w;V)\|\leq C(1+\|V\|+|\xi_{k}|+\|u\|+\|w\|)^{C}. (30)

Here derivatives are with respect to (u,w)(u,w), and any fixed norm on the finite collection of deeper-layer matrices may be used for ‖V‖\|V\|. For example, Dw​𝔖k​(u,w,V)=−D​𝒢V​(u)⊤​D​𝝋​(w)D_{w}\mathfrak{S}_{k}(u,w;V)=-D\mathscr{G}_{V}(u)^{\top}D\bm{\varphi}(w); this derivative does not contain the residual as a factor. The fourth activation derivative and the third link derivative suffice for (30). Since |χR​(x)|≤C​|x||\chi_{R}(x)|\leq C|x| and ‖χR(j)‖∞≤C\|\chi_{R}^{(j)}\|_{\infty}\leq C for 1≤j≤31\leq j\leq 3, the same polynomial bound holds for the cutoff map, uniformly in R≥1R\geq 1. Also, bounded activation derivatives imply the sharper value bound

‖𝔖k​(u,w,V)‖+‖𝔖ˇs,k,R​(u,w)‖≤C​κC​(1+‖u‖+‖w‖C),\|\mathfrak{S}_{k}(u,w;V)\|+\|\check{\mathfrak{S}}_{s,k,R}(u,w)\|\leq C\kappa^{C}(1+\|u\|+\|w\|^{C}), (31)

once the original V(s−1)V^{(s-1)} is bounded by a polynomial in κ\kappa.

We establish this polynomial bound jointly with the state-evolution moment bounds, using the derivative estimates above so that the constants remain uniform in RR. With the same column-vector convention, put

Ps,k​(x)\displaystyle P_{s,k}(x) =𝔖k​(Θk(s)​(x),x(0),V(s−1)),\displaystyle=\mathfrak{S}_{k}\bigl(\Theta_{k}^{(s)}(x),x^{(0)};V^{(s-1)}\bigr),
Js,j,k​(x)\displaystyle J_{s,j,k}(x) =Dx(j)​Θk(s)​(x),Ks,j,k​(x)=Dx(j)​Ps,k​(x).\displaystyle=D_{x^{(j)}}\Theta_{k}^{(s)}(x),\qquad K_{s,j,k}(x)=D_{x^{(j)}}P_{s,k}(x).

The state evolution for the cutoff iteration follows from the generic asymmetric GFOM recursion in HI25 Definition , with time shifted by one so that the deterministic initial states are u(−1)u^{(-1)} and v(−1)v^{(-1)}. For each input coordinate i∈[n]i\in[n], write the Gaussian innovation as a row 𝔙ˇi(s)∈ℝ1×q\check{\mathfrak{V}}_{i}^{(s)}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times q}. The corresponding column state satisfies

Under the conditions and notation of Lemma S.1.1, let (u^(s),v^(s))(\hat{u}^{(s)},\hat{v}^{(s)}) and (u(s),v(s))(u^{(s)},v^{(s)}) denote the actual and auxiliary iterates, respectively. We again work conditionally on 𝒢a\mathcal{G}_{a} and use the Gaussian moment bounds and auxiliary comparison proved in Lemma S.1.2.

It is therefore pseudo-Lipschitz in (z,w)(z,w) of a fixed order, uniformly in kk, with a constant polynomial in 1+‖V‖+‖ξ‖∞1+\|V\|+\|\xi\|_{\infty}. Define the auxiliary gradient error

Δs=max2≤α≤L⁡‖1m​∑k=1m𝒟α,k​(uk(s+1),uk(0),V(s))−Mα(s)‖.\Delta_{s}=\max_{2\leq\alpha\leq L}\left\|\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\mathcal{D}_{\alpha,k}(u_{k}^{(s+1)},u_{k}^{(0)},V^{(s)})-M_{\alpha}^{(s)}\right\|.

The definition of Mα(s)M_{\alpha}^{(s)} is the corresponding Gaussian expectation. Apply Lemma S.1.2 entrywise to this fixed collection of pseudo-Lipschitz functions. For each fixed r≥1r\geq 1,

𝔼Δsr≤(Cκlogn)Cn−1/C.\mathbb{E}\Delta_{s}^{r}\leq(C\kappa\log n)^{C}n^{-1/C}. (43)

The constants may depend on T,rT,r, and this convention applies throughout the rest of the proof.

Put

We first compare the corrected empirical risk with a risk evaluated at an independent Gaussian context and a noise value sampled uniformly from the realized arm-wise noise values. Definition E.2 (Test functions for weighted averages).

Fix a∈[K]a\in[K] and t∈ℤ≥0t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. |Φt,k​(0,w,s)|\displaystyle|\Phi_{t,k}(0,w,s)| ≤La,t​(1+‖w‖p).\displaystyle\leq L_{a,t}(1+\|w\|^{p}).

Moreover, with
