the family {ΘΦ,t,k}k=1N\{\Theta_{\Phi,t,k}\}_{k=1}^{N} satisfies the following pseudo-Lipschitz and origin bounds with the same pp and La,tL_{a,t}:

𝒪^a(t)​(Φrisk)=ℰ^a(t),𝒪a,π(t)​(Φrisk)=ℰa,π(t).\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{a}^{(t)}(\Phi^{\mathrm{risk}})=\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)},\qquad\mathcal{O}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}(\Phi^{\mathrm{risk}})=\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}.

Proposition S.3 gives (62). For fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and r≥1r\geq 1, conditional Markov’s inequality and a union bound yield

Each integrand in the sum is bounded by one and converges in probability to zero by (19); hence, its expectation converges to zero. Since ℙ⁡(Ecntc)→0\mathbb{P}(E_{\mathrm{cnt}}^{c})\to 0, this proves the final display. ∎

Appendix F Independent Noise and Fitted-Value Comparisons

The preceding risk comparison uses the empirical distribution of the training noises. We first bound prediction moments, then replace this distribution with the arm-specific noise law to obtain conditional test risk. We also derive the comparison of weighted fitted predictions used in the ADM and ADR proofs.

F.1 Prediction moments

Proposition F.1 (Fixed-grid prediction moment bound).

Assume the conditions of Section C, with m/d→ϕ∈(0,∞)m/d\to\phi\in(0,\infty) and fixed K,L,q,𝒯K,L,q,\mathcal{T}. For every arm a∈[K]a\in[K] and Z∼N⁡(0,Id)Z\sim N(0,I_{d}) independent of ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, as d→∞d\to\infty,

supt∈𝒯𝔼[|fWa(t)(Z)|2|𝒟m,Wa(0)]=dop​(1).\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}\left[|f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z)|^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}\right]=d^{o_{p}(1)}. (63)
Proof.

On EcntE_{\mathrm{cnt}}, the arm-wise forms of HI25 Proposition  and HI25 Proposition  give, uniformly on the fixed grid,

∥Wa,1(t)∥F=dop​(1),maxα∈[2:L]∥Wa,α(t)∥op=dop​(1).\|W_{a,1}^{(t)}\|_{F}=d^{o_{p}(1)},\qquad\max_{\alpha\in[2:L]}\|W_{a,\alpha}^{(t)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=d^{o_{p}(1)}.

|fWa(t)(z)|≤CtκWa,[2:L](t)Ct{1+∥z⊤Wa,1(t)∥∞}.|f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(z)|\leq C_{t}\kappa_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}^{C_{t}}\{1+\|z^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)}\|_{\infty}\}.

Conditional on (𝒟m,Wa(0))(\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}), the fitted matrices are fixed and Z⊤​Wa,1(t)Z^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)} is Gaussian. Since qq is fixed,

𝔼[∥Z⊤Wa,1(t)∥∞2|𝒟m,Wa(0)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|Z^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)}\|_{\infty}^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}\right] ≤∑j=1q𝔼[|Z⊤(Wa,1(t))⋅j|2|𝒟m,Wa(0)]\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathbb{E}\left[|Z^{\top}(W_{a,1}^{(t)})_{\cdot j}|^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}\right]
=∑j=1q‖(Wa,1(t))⋅j‖22=‖Wa,1(t)‖F2.\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\|(W_{a,1}^{(t)})_{\cdot j}\|_{2}^{2}=\|W_{a,1}^{(t)}\|_{F}^{2}.

Therefore, after changing CtC_{t},

𝔼[|fWa(t)(Z)|2|𝒟m,Wa(0)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[|f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z)|^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}\right] ≤CtκWa,[2:L](t)Ct{1+∥Wa,1(t)∥F2}=dop​(1)\displaystyle\leq C_{t}\kappa_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}^{C_{t}}\{1+\|W_{a,1}^{(t)}\|_{F}^{2}\}=d^{o_{p}(1)}

on EcntE_{\mathrm{cnt}}, uniformly over the fixed grid 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Since ℙ⁡(Ecntc)→0\mathbb{P}(E_{\mathrm{cnt}}^{c})\to 0, this proves (63). ∎

F.3 Corrected predictions on logged actions

For a∈[K]a\in[K] and t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, define

Ma(t)\displaystyle M_{a}^{(t)} ≔𝔼[wa(Z)fWa(t)(Z)|𝒟m,Wa(0)],\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[w_{a}(Z)f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z)\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}\right],

Proposition F.3 (Weighted averages of corrected predictions).

Assume the conditions of Section C, with fixed K,L,q,𝒯K,L,q,\mathcal{T}. For every a∈[K]a\in[K], t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, and r≥1r\geq 1, on EcntE_{\mathrm{cnt}},

=𝔼[wa(Z)fWa(t)(Z)|𝒟m,Wa(0)]=Ma(t).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[w_{a}(Z)f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z)\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}\right]=M_{a}^{(t)}.

Appendix G Uniform Consistency and Model Selection

We combine the arm-wise risk comparisons to prove uniform consistency of the risk criterion over the fixed iterate grid. We then derive the oracle inequality for model selection and the resulting bound on policy value error.

G.1 Proof of Theorem 4.1

See 4.1

Proof.

Fix an arm aa. By Proposition E.3,

supt∈𝒯|ℰ^a(t)−ℰa,π(t)|→𝑝0.\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0.

By Proposition F.2,

supt∈𝒯|ℰa,π(t)−ℰa,ind(t)|→𝑝0.\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0.

Therefore

supt∈𝒯|ℰ^a(t)−ℰa,ind(t)|≤supt∈𝒯|ℰ^a(t)−ℰa,π(t)|+supt∈𝒯|ℰa,π(t)−ℰa,ind(t)|,\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert\leq\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}\right\rvert+\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert,

and the right-hand side is op​(1)o_{p}(1). This proves the theorem. ∎

G.2 Risk decomposition and a bound on policy value error

Recall that, for deterministic measurable gg,

ℛν∘​(g)=𝔼​∑a=1Kν⁡(a|X)​{g⁡(X,a)−g∗​(X,a)}2.\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g)=\mathbb{E}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X)\{g(X,a)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\}^{2}.

For an ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}-measurable predictor, the expectation is conditional on ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}} and uses an independent test observation, as in Section C.

Proposition G.1 (Prediction risk bounds policy value error).

Assume known context-independent logging with μ⁡(a)>0\mu(a)>0 for every arm, let g∗(X,A)=𝔼[R|X,A]g^{\ast}(X,A)=\mathbb{E}[R\,|\,X,A], and suppose 𝔼⁡[R2]<∞\mathbb{E}[R^{2}]<\infty. For every deterministic measurable or ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}-measurable predictor gg satisfying ℛν∘​(g)<∞\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g)<\infty almost surely,

|𝒱g​(ν)−𝒱​(ν)|\displaystyle|\mathcal{V}_{g}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)| ≤ℛν∘​(g),\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g)},
ℛν​(g)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g) =ℛν​(g∗)+ℛν∘​(g).\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g^{\ast})+\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g).
Proof of Proposition G.1.

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} denote either the trivial sigma-field or ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, let g~\tilde{g} be ℋ\mathcal{H}-measurable, and let (X,A,R)(X,A,R) be an independent test draw. Since the logging policy is context independent,

𝒱g~​(ν)−𝒱​(ν)\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\tilde{g}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu) =𝔼⁡[∑a=1Kν⁡(a|X)​(g~​(X,a)−g∗​(X,a))|ℋ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X)\left(\tilde{g}(X,a)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\right)\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]
=𝔼⁡[wA​(X)​(g~​(X,A)−g∗​(X,A))|ℋ].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\left(\tilde{g}(X,A)-g^{\ast}(X,A)\right)\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right].

Conditional Cauchy–Schwarz yields

|𝒱g~​(ν)−𝒱⁡(ν)|\displaystyle\left\lvert\mathcal{V}_{\tilde{g}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right\rvert ≤𝔼​[wA​(X)|ℋ]1/2​𝔼​[wA​(X)​(g~​(X,A)−g∗​(X,A))2|ℋ]1/2.\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\left(\tilde{g}(X,A)-g^{\ast}(X,A)\right)^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]^{1/2}.

The first factor equals one because

𝔼[wA(X)|X,ℋ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[w_{A}(X)\,|\,X,\mathcal{H}] =∑a=1Kμ⁡(a)​ν⁡(a|X)μ⁡(a)=1,\displaystyle=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\mu(a)\frac{\nu(a\,|\,X)}{\mu(a)}=1,

and the square of the second factor is

This proves the value bound.

For the risk decomposition, write ε≔R−g∗​(X,A)\varepsilon\coloneqq R-g^{\ast}(X,A) and δg~​(X,A)≔g∗​(X,A)−g~​(X,A)\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A)\coloneqq g^{\ast}(X,A)-\tilde{g}(X,A). Then, R−g~​(X,A)=ε+δg~​(X,A)R-\tilde{g}(X,A)=\varepsilon+\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A), and expanding the square yields

ℛν​(g~)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(\tilde{g}) =𝔼⁡[wA​(X)​ε2|ℋ]+𝔼⁡[wA​(X)​δg~​(X,A)2|ℋ]+2​𝔼​[wA​(X)​ε​δg~​(X,A)|ℋ].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\varepsilon^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A)^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]+2\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\varepsilon\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A)\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right].

The cross term is zero, since iterated conditioning yields

𝔼[wA(X)εδg~(X,A)|ℋ]=𝔼[wA(X)δg~(X,A)𝔼[ε|X,A,ℋ]|ℋ]=0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\varepsilon\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A)\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A)\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\,|\,X,A,\mathcal{H}]\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]=0.

The first remaining term is ℛν​(g∗)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g^{\ast}) and the second is ℛν∘​(g~)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(\tilde{g}), proving the decomposition. Taking ℋ\mathcal{H} to be trivial gives the deterministic statement, while taking ℋ=ℱtr\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}} gives its conditional out-of-sample version. ∎

These finite-sample conclusions use only the logging probabilities and the conditional mean of the reward; they do not require the neural-network assumptions.

G.4 Suboptimal stopping after full-data refitting

With a fixed validation fraction, cross-validation estimates the test risk of models trained at a different limiting sample-to-dimension ratio. The following example shows that ten-fold cross-validation can correctly rank these models yet select a suboptimal iterate after full-data refitting.

Let F1,…,F10F_{1},\ldots,F_{10} partition [m][m] independently of the observations, with |Fj|=m/10+o⁡(m)|F_{j}|=m/10+o(m). Write ga,t(−j)g_{a,t}^{(-j)} for the arm-aa model trained on ℐa∖Fj\mathcal{I}_{a}\setminus F_{j}, using the same initialization and learning rates as the full-data model ga,tg_{a,t}. On 𝒯={0,1}\mathcal{T}=\{0,1\}, define

ℰ^aCV​(t)≔1Na​∑j=110∑i∈ℐa∩Fj{Ri−ga,t(−j)​(Xi)}2,t^aCV∈arg⁡mint∈𝒯​ℰ^aCV​(t).\widehat{\mathcal{E}}^{\rm CV}_{a}(t)\coloneqq\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{j=1}^{10}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}\cap F_{j}}\{R_{i}-g_{a,t}^{(-j)}(X_{i})\}^{2},\qquad\hat{t}_{a}^{\rm CV}\in\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\widehat{\mathcal{E}}^{\rm CV}_{a}(t).

The importance weights equal one in the example below. Let ta⋆∈arg⁡mint∈𝒯​ℛν,a∘​(ga,t)t_{a}^{\star}\in\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a,t}) be the full-data risk minimizer, and set 𝐭^CV=(t^1CV,…,t^KCV)\hat{\mathbf{t}}^{\rm CV}=(\hat{t}_{1}^{\rm CV},\ldots,\hat{t}_{K}^{\rm CV}). Break ties toward t=0t=0 and use any measurable convention when a required arm count is zero; the latter event has probability tending to zero.

Proposition G.2 (Suboptimal stopping after cross-validation).

Let Xi​∼iid​N​(0,Id)X_{i}\overset{\rm iid}{\sim}N(0,I_{d}), let K≥2K\geq 2 be fixed, and assume context-independent logging with μ⁡(a)=ν⁡(a∣x)=1/K\mu(a)=\nu(a\mid x)=1/K and m/d→Km/d\to K. Take noiseless rewards Ri=g∗​(Xi,Ai)=β⊤​XiR_{i}=g^{\ast}(X_{i},A_{i})=\beta^{\top}X_{i}, where β=d−1/2(1,…,1)⊤\beta=d^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^{\top}. The example satisfies the working assumptions: the reward link and activation are identity maps, the noise is zero, the importance weights are constant, and d​‖β‖∞=1\sqrt{d}\,\|\beta\|_{\infty}=1 with bounded initializations. Appendix H Value Estimation Without Sample Splitting and Consequences

We now prove that ADM consistently estimates 𝒱g𝐭​(ν)\mathcal{V}_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(\nu) and ADR consistently estimates 𝒱⁡(ν)\mathcal{V}(\nu) when both are evaluated on the reward-model training sample. For each arm, the proof treats predictions on that arm’s training observations using the Onsager correction. Predictions on observations assigned to other arms satisfy conditional laws of large numbers. In the ADR estimator, the resulting conditional expectations of the fitted predictions cancel.

For a,b∈[K]a,b\in[K] and t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, define

where Z∼N⁡(0,Id)Z\sim N(0,I_{d}) is independent of ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Assume the conditions of Section C, with m/d→ϕ∈(0,∞)m/d\to\phi\in(0,\infty) and fixed K,L,q,𝒯K,L,q,\mathcal{T}. Then, as d→∞d\to\infty,

Under the sub-Gaussian noise condition in Assumption 2.2, the reward-average bound strengthens to Op(d−1/2)O_{p}(d^{-1/2}).

Proof.

The diagonal fitted-value bound follows from Proposition F.3 and a finite union over the arms. For a≠ba\neq b, let

ℱ^b≔σ⁡(ℐb,Xℐb,Rℐb,Wb(0)),\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{b}\coloneqq\sigma(\mathcal{I}_{b},X_{\mathcal{I}_{b}},R_{\mathcal{I}_{b}},W_{b}^{(0)}),

and let

ℱ^a,b≔σ⁡(A1,…,Am,Xℐb,Rℐb,Wb(0)).\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}\coloneqq\sigma(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m},X_{\mathcal{I}_{b}},R_{\mathcal{I}_{b}},W_{b}^{(0)}).

The count event EcntE_{\mathrm{cnt}} is measurable with respect to ℱ^a,b\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}. For the off-diagonal comparison, work on this event, so Na≥1N_{a}\geq 1. Conditional on ℱ^a,b\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}, the arm-bb predictor is fixed, while {Xi:i∈ℐa}\{X_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}\} are i.i.d. N⁡(0,Id)N(0,I_{d}) and independent of that predictor. Because ZZ is independent of ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, the definition of Mb(t)M_{b}^{(t)} is unchanged if ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}} is replaced by ℱ^b\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{b}; hence, Mb(t)M_{b}^{(t)} is ℱ^a,b\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}-measurable. Boundedness of wbw_{b} and Proposition F.1 therefore give

≤1Na​𝔼​[|Yi,b(t)|2|ℱ^a,b]≤d−1+op​(1),\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{N_{a}}\mathbb{E}\left[|Y_{i,b}^{(t)}|^{2}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}\right]\leq d^{-1+o_{p}(1)}, (71)

For the count bound, Na∼Binomial⁡(m,μ⁡(a))N_{a}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,\mu(a)), so

where CC is uniform in dd because m≍dm\asymp d and KK is fixed. Letting M→∞M\to\infty proves the third claim.

For the reward-average comparison, continue to work on EcntE_{\mathrm{cnt}}. Decompose

≤Bh2Na​‖ξℐa‖∞2≤Bh2c−​d​ϰ∗,a2=d−1+op​(1)\displaystyle\leq\frac{B_{h}^{2}}{N_{a}}\|\xi_{\mathcal{I}_{a}}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq\frac{B_{h}^{2}}{c_{-}d}\varkappa_{\ast,a}^{2}=d^{-1+o_{p}(1)}

Proof of Theorem 4.4.

For i∈ℐai\in\mathcal{I}_{a}, abbreviate the corrected observed-action prediction by

ci,a(t)≔GWa,[2:L](t)(U^i,a(t)).c_{i,a}^{(t)}\coloneqq G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}(\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)}).

BM\displaystyle B_{M} ≔max⁡supt∈𝒯a∈[K]⁡|Ma(t)|.\displaystyle\coloneqq\max_{a\in[K]}\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|M_{a}^{(t)}|.

By Lemma H.1,

δdiag=op(1),δoff=op(1),δN=Op(d−1/2),δR=op(1),BM=dop​(1).\delta_{\mathrm{diag}}=o_{p}(1),\quad\delta_{\mathrm{off}}=o_{p}(1),\quad\delta_{N}=O_{p}(d^{-1/2}),\quad\delta_{R}=o_{p}(1),\quad B_{M}=d^{o_{p}(1)}. (72)
ADM.

For i∈ℐai\in\mathcal{I}_{a}, (8) and ν⁡(b|x)=μ⁡(b)​wb​(x)\nu(b\,|\,x)=\mu(b)w_{b}(x) give the rowwise identity

∑b=1Kν⁡(b|Xi)​g^𝐭​(Xi,b)\displaystyle\sum_{b=1}^{K}\nu(b\,|\,X_{i})\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{t}}(X_{i},b) =∑b≠aμ⁡(b)​wb​(Xi)​fWb(tb)​(Xi)+μ⁡(a)​wa​(Xi)​ci,a(ta).\displaystyle=\sum_{b\neq a}\mu(b)w_{b}(X_{i})f_{W_{b}^{(t_{b})}}(X_{i})+\mu(a)w_{a}(X_{i})c_{i,a}^{(t_{a})}.

Summing first within each logged-action set and then over the arms yields

𝒱^ADM​(𝐭)=∑a=1KNam​[∑b≠aμ⁡(b)​M¯a,b(tb)+μ⁡(a)​M^a,diag(ta)].\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\frac{N_{a}}{m}\left[\sum_{b\neq a}\mu(b)\,\overline{M}_{a,b}^{(t_{b})}+\mu(a)\,\widehat{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t_{a})}\right]. (73)

Let

+∑a=1K{Nam−μ(a)}∑b=1Kμ(b)Mb(tb).\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{a=1}^{K}\left\{\frac{N_{a}}{m}-\mu(a)\right\}\sum_{b=1}^{K}\mu(b)M_{b}^{(t_{b})}.

The second sum is zero because ∑aNa/m=∑aμ⁡(a)=1\sum_{a}N_{a}/m=\sum_{a}\mu(a)=1. Since the weights in the first sum are nonnegative,

sup𝐭∈𝒯K|𝒱^ADM​(𝐭)−TADM​(𝐭)|\displaystyle\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}|\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})-T_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})| ≤∑a=1KNam​{(1−μ⁡(a))​δoff+μ⁡(a)​δdiag}\displaystyle\leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\frac{N_{a}}{m}\{(1-\mu(a))\delta_{\mathrm{off}}+\mu(a)\delta_{\mathrm{diag}}\}

uniformly over 𝐭∈𝒯K\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}.

Now

ADR.

=op​(1)\displaystyle=o_{p}(1)

by (72) and δN​BM=op​(1)\delta_{N}B_{M}=o_{p}(1). Therefore

uniformly over 𝐭∈𝒯K\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}.

∎

Corollary H.2 (Uniform ADM–ADR comparison).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.4, the estimators in (9) and (10) satisfy, as d→∞d\to\infty,

H.1 Error of uncorrected same-sample DR

We first recall the empirical-process condition used in classical analyses of DR estimators. We then examine whether this condition holds over the neural-network class considered here and derive the estimation error along the fitted gradient-descent trajectory. Let Pm,dP_{m,d} be the empirical measure of the training sample. Consider the DR estimator obtained by substituting the fitted networks g𝐭g_{\mathbf{t}} into ψg\psi_{g} and averaging over their training sample, without the Onsager correction:

𝒱^DRnv​(𝐭)≔1m​∑i=1mψg𝐭​(Qi).\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\mathbf{t})\coloneqq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\psi_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(Q_{i}). (78)

Define Hg,d​(Q)≔ψg​(Q)−ψg∗​(Q)H_{g,d}(Q)\coloneqq\psi_{g}(Q)-\psi_{g^{\ast}}(Q). Known context-independent logging gives Pd​Hg,d=0P_{d}H_{g,d}=0 for every realized integrable ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}-measurable gg. Consequently, the exact decomposition

m​{𝒱^DRnv​(𝐭)−𝒱⁡(ν)}=𝔾m,d​{ψg∗−𝒱⁡(ν)}+𝔾m,d​Hg𝐭,d\sqrt{m}\{\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\}=\mathbb{G}_{m,d}\{\psi_{g^{\ast}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\}+\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H_{g_{\mathbf{t}},d}

holds for the training-measurable fitted model g𝐭g_{\mathbf{t}}.

Remark H.3 (Donsker conditions and cross-fitting).

When the data distribution PP is fixed, asymptotic stochastic equicontinuity yields 𝔾m​Hg^=op​(1)\mathbb{G}_{m}H_{\widehat{g}}=o_{p}(1) if, with probability tending to one, Hg^H_{\widehat{g}} belongs to a fixed PP-Donsker class and ‖Hg^‖P,2=op​(1)\|H_{\widehat{g}}\|_{P,2}=o_{p}(1). Cross-fitting evaluates each fitted reward model on observations excluded from its training sample. For each fold, conditional on its fitted model, the evaluation observations are independent with law PP. With a fixed number of folds, conditional Chebyshev’s inequality therefore makes the cross-fitted empirical-process term op​(1)o_{p}(1) when each fitted score error converges to zero in L2​(P)L^{2}(P), without a Donsker condition [Chernozhukov et al., 2018]. A fixed iterate grid gives finitely many models for each realized training sample. It does not put those models in a fixed Donsker class: as the data vary, each iterate ranges over a class whose input dimension grows with dd.

The next proposition yields a sequence of classes whose functions converge uniformly to zero in L2​(Pd)L^{2}(P_{d}), but whose empirical-process supremum does not converge to zero. Thus, local stochastic equicontinuity fails over the full class of permitted predictors. This does not determine the error of the particular predictors produced by gradient descent, which we analyze separately below.

Consider the admissible submodel g∗=0g^{\ast}=0 and ν=μ\nu=\mu. For a fixed arm a∈[K]a\in[K], define

gθ,d​(x,b)\displaystyle g_{\theta,d}(x,b) ≔𝟏{b=a}θ⊤x,∥θ∥2≤d−1/2,\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbf{1}\{b=a\}\theta^{\top}x,\qquad\|\theta\|_{2}\leq d^{-1/2},
Hθ,d​(Q)\displaystyle H_{\theta,d}(Q) ≔ψgθ,d​(Q)−ψg∗​(Q)={μ⁡(a)−𝟏​(A=a)}​θ⊤​X,\displaystyle\coloneqq\psi_{g_{\theta,d}}(Q)-\psi_{g^{\ast}}(Q)=\{\mu(a)-\mathbf{1}(A=a)\}\theta^{\top}X,

and let ℋd≔{Hθ,d:∥θ∥2≤d−1/2}\mathcal{H}_{d}\coloneqq\{H_{\theta,d}:\|\theta\|_{2}\leq d^{-1/2}\}.

Proposition H.4 (Failure of local stochastic equicontinuity).

Under the Gaussian design and known logging conditions in Assumptions 2.2 and 2.1, with fixed K≥2K\geq 2 and m/d→ϕ∈(0,∞)m/d\to\phi\in(0,\infty), the class ℋd\mathcal{H}_{d} satisfies

supH∈ℋd|𝔾m,d​H|\displaystyle\sup_{H\in\mathcal{H}_{d}}|\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H| →𝑝μ⁡(a)​{1−μ⁡(a)}.\displaystyle\xrightarrow{p}\sqrt{\mu(a)\{1-\mu(a)\}}.

Independence of AA and XX gives

The result follows from ‖Zd‖2/d→𝑝1\|Z_{d}\|_{2}/\sqrt{d}\xrightarrow{p}1 for Zd∼N⁡(0,Id)Z_{d}\sim N(0,I_{d}). ∎

Remark H.5.

The predictors in Proposition H.4 are represented by the permitted network with depth two, width one, and identity activation: take W1=θW_{1}=\theta and W2=1W_{2}=1. The architecture and scaling assumptions therefore do not imply local stochastic equicontinuity over the entire predictor class.

This contradicts tightness. If a class ℋd\mathcal{H}_{d} contains the fitted score error with probability tending to one, then

ℙ⁡(|𝔾m,d​H𝐭^d,d|>M)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}|>M\right) ≤ℙ⁡(H𝐭^d,d∉ℋd)+ℙ⁡(supH∈ℋd|𝔾m,d​H|>M).\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}(H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}\notin\mathcal{H}_{d})+\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{H\in\mathcal{H}_{d}}|\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H|>M\right).

Thus, the stated uniform class bound would imply tightness and cannot hold. ∎

The preceding result applies when the DR estimation error does not converge to zero. The following example satisfies this condition after a single gradient-descent update.

In the nonparametric model with known logging probabilities and unrestricted context and reward distributions, ψg∗−𝒱⁡(ν)\psi_{g^{\ast}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu) is the efficient influence function [Kennedy, 2024]. The Gaussian single-index model considered here imposes additional restrictions, so its efficiency bound requires a separate calculation. The notation σeff2\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2} in Corollary 4.5 denotes the variance of ψg∗\psi_{g^{\ast}}.

The state-evolution results in this paper assume that the arm-wise aspect ratios stay bounded above and away from zero, with fixed network width and training horizon. Extending these results to m/d→∞m/d\to\infty, growing width, or a growing training horizon requires new bounds that are uniform in the corresponding parameters.

H.2 Variance of the DR score on an independent observation

We evaluate ψg​(X,A,R)\psi_{g}(X,A,R) on an observation independent of the sample used to fit gg. Conditional on ℱtr\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, this score has mean 𝒱⁡(ν)\mathcal{V}(\nu) under the known logging policy. The next proposition decomposes its conditional variance and bounds the part that depends on gg by the target-policy-weighted prediction risk. To obtain the sampling variance of ADR, one must also account for covariances between the adjusted terms evaluated on different training observations.

For an independent observation (X,A,R)(X,A,R) and a reward model gg, define

vintrinsic​(X)\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{intrinsic}}(X) ≔∑a=1Kν​(a|X)2μ⁡(a)​σξ,a2,\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\frac{\nu(a\,|\,X)^{2}}{\mu(a)}\sigma_{\xi,a}^{2},

Vintrinsic\displaystyle V_{\mathrm{intrinsic}} ≔Var⁡{ψg∗​(X,A,R)},\displaystyle\coloneqq\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{g^{\ast}}(X,A,R)\},
𝒥var​(g)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{var}}(g) ≔𝔼⁡[Vmodel​(X,g)|ℱtr],\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[V_{\mathrm{model}}(X,g)\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}],
𝒥DR​(g)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}}(g) ≔𝔼⁡[∑a=1Kν⁡(a|X)​1−μ⁡(a)μ⁡(a)​{g⁡(X,a)−g∗​(X,a)}2|ℱtr].\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X)\frac{1-\mu(a)}{\mu(a)}\{g(X,a)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\}^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}\right].

For deterministic gg, the conditioning in these definitions can be omitted. Also set

c−​(μ)≔mina∈[K]⁡1−μ⁡(a)μ⁡(a),c+​(μ)≔maxa∈[K]⁡1−μ⁡(a)μ⁡(a).c_{-}(\mu)\coloneqq\min_{a\in[K]}\frac{1-\mu(a)}{\mu(a)},\qquad c_{+}(\mu)\coloneqq\max_{a\in[K]}\frac{1-\mu(a)}{\mu(a)}.

Appendix J Additional Experiments and Implementation Details

J.1 Synthetic data and network training

Unless stated otherwise, the Gaussian experiments use independent observations with Xi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)X_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), Ai∼Unif⁡([K])A_{i}\sim\operatorname{Unif}([K]), and εi∼𝒩⁡(0,0.82)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.8^{2}), where the contexts, actions, and noises are mutually independent. The rewards are

Ri=φAi∗​(βAi⊤​Xi)+εi.R_{i}=\varphi_{A_{i}}^{\ast}(\beta_{A_{i}}^{\top}X_{i})+\varepsilon_{i}.

The two-arm baseline uses φ1∗​(y)=tanh⁡(y)\varphi_{1}^{\ast}(y)=\tanh(y), φ2∗​(y)=tanh⁡(2​y)\varphi_{2}^{\ast}(y)=\tanh(2y), and the logistic target policy ν⁡(1∣x)=σ⁡(2​β1⊤​x)\nu(1\mid x)=\sigma(2\beta_{1}^{\top}x), where σ⁡(u)=(1+e−u)−1\sigma(u)=(1+e^{-u})^{-1}. The signal directions are fixed, dense, and orthonormal. Other reward links and policies are specified below.

For each arm, we train the network in Appendix C with sigmoid activation, depth L=2L=2, and width q=5q=5. First-layer entries are initialized independently from 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d) and deeper-layer entries from 𝒩⁡(0,1/q)\mathcal{N}(0,1/q), with columns 2,…,q2,\ldots,q of the output matrix set to zero. Initial weights are fixed across datasets and shared by all procedures and folds. Every layer is updated by full-batch gradient descent on the unweighted loss ℒa\mathcal{L}_{a}, normalized by its arm-specific training count except in the leave-one-out diagnostic below. Candidate times are 𝒯={0,…,30}\mathcal{T}=\{0,\ldots,30\}. We use η=2\eta=2 unless stated otherwise; the increasing-ratio experiment uses η=1\eta=1 for every method.

J.2 Stopping rules and comparison estimators

For a full-data model, the proposed stopping rule minimizes (6) separately for each arm. We compare it with the rule that minimizes the criterion obtained by replacing the corrected predictions with fWa(t)​(Xi)f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(X_{i}), and with ten-fold cross-validation. In the experiment with several target policies, we also minimize the corrected criterion with wa≡1w_{a}\equiv 1 to isolate the effect of weighting the stopping rule for the target policy. All rules choose the smallest minimizing iteration. For cross-validation, a random partition of the complete logged sample defines the folds independently of the observations. We train each arm’s network on the complement of each fold and pool its weighted squared residuals over the held-out observations from that arm. The selected number of steps is then used to fit the model on the full arm sample from the common initialization. Consequently, every stopping rule is evaluated on the same full-data training trajectory. Its selection regret is

ℛν∘​(g𝐭^)−min𝐭∈𝒯K⁡ℛν∘​(g𝐭).\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}})-\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\mathbf{t}}).

The minimum separates over arms. The reward-noise contribution does not depend on the stopping times, so the same regret is obtained using ℛν\mathcal{R}_{\nu}.

For risk estimation in Figures 1 and 9, we compare the criterion with ℰa,ind(t)\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)} in (11), including the reward-noise contribution. The reported RMSE is the square root of the mean squared discrepancy, where the mean is taken over arms, candidate iterations, and datasets. Selection regret is reported on the total target-risk scale.

For ten-fold cross-fitting (CF10), we randomly partition the complete logged sample into ten folds independently of the observations. Corrected stopping minimizes (6) on each arm’s complete training-complement path. For inner-validation stopping, we split the complement within each arm into 70%70\% for training and 30%30\% for selection. These partitions are independent of the contexts and rewards. We select by held-out weighted squared residuals, restart from the common initialization, and refit on the complete arm-specific complement. Both procedures use the same folds and candidate iterations, exclude the evaluation fold from fitting and selection, and average ordinary held-out DR scores with augmentation coefficient one.

The inverse propensity scoring (IPS) and self-normalized inverse propensity scoring (SNIPS) estimators use the same logged sample:

𝒱^IPS=1m​∑i=1mwAi​(Xi)​Ri,𝒱^SNIPS=∑i=1mwAi​(Xi)​Ri∑i=1mwAi​(Xi).\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{IPS}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})R_{i},\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{SNIPS}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})R_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})}.

For the direct comparison of the Onsager correction, we evaluate the DR estimator in (78) and ADR at identical full-data models and stopping times. We likewise compare ADM with the unadjusted empirical average of the same fitted predictions. The target in this latter comparison is 𝒱g𝐭^​(ν)\mathcal{V}_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu), evaluated separately for each fitted model.

We also evaluate each arm’s selected predictor on contexts logged under other arms, without changing its training sample or stopping time:

𝒱^cross=∑a=1K1m−Na​∑i∉ℐaν⁡(a∣Xi)​fWa(t^a)​(Xi).\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{cross}}=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\frac{1}{m-N_{a}}\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{I}_{a}}\nu(a\mid X_{i})f_{W_{a}^{(\hat{t}_{a})}}(X_{i}). (88)

Here t^a\hat{t}_{a} is selected by the corrected criterion using only arm-aa data. Under context-independent logging, conditional on the action labels, the other arms’ contexts are independent of this fitted predictor; this is the off-diagonal independence argument in Lemma H.1. The denominator is the actual number m−Nam-N_{a} of evaluation contexts. Like DM and ADM in this comparison, cross-arm DM targets the fitted-model value 𝒱g𝐭^​(ν)\mathcal{V}_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu), rather than the true policy value.

Figure 3 compares these estimators on the same 200 datasets and selected models per dimension. ADM reduces MSE relative to cross-arm DM by 50.7%50.7\%–57.4%57.4\%; all five paired pointwise 95%95\% intervals favor ADM. Both estimators’ bias intervals contain zero in every setting. The gain is therefore in precision for the fitted-model value.

J.3 Vanishing-fraction holdouts

We compare two holdout sizes fixed before running the experiment, h=⌈m⌉h=\lceil\sqrt{m}\rceil and h=⌈m2/3⌉h=\lceil m^{2/3}\rceil, on the same five Gaussian, uniform-logging settings and 200 datasets per dimension as Figure 1. Both satisfy h→∞h\to\infty and h/m→0h/m\to 0. For each dataset, one permutation independent of the observations defines nested holdouts of these sizes. Each arm’s network is trained on its complement from the common initialization. We average weighted squared residuals over that arm’s held-out observations and select the smallest minimizing iteration. The selected iteration is then evaluated on the same full-data trajectory as the other stopping rules, corresponding to full-data refitting.

Table 1 reports the risk-estimation RMSE and selection regret defined in Appendix J.2. Both holdouts have larger errors and regret than the corrected criterion and ten-fold CV at every dimension. For both metrics, all paired pointwise 95%95\% intervals favor the corrected criterion and CV over the holdouts; risk-estimation comparisons use MSE. Intervals use within-dataset differences, as described in Appendix J.9. The two schedules thus show a finite-sample accuracy–cost trade-off: correction is more accurate, while the holdouts are cheaper (Appendix J.11); their asymptotic comparison remains open.

J.4 Target-policy weighting

Figure 2 uses three arms with reward links φ1∗​(y)=12+tanh⁡(y)+12​tanh2⁡(y)\varphi_{1}^{\ast}(y)=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tanh(y)+\tfrac{1}{2}\tanh^{2}(y), φ2∗​(y)=−12+tanh⁡(2​y)−12​tanh2⁡(y)\varphi_{2}^{\ast}(y)=-\tfrac{1}{2}+\tanh(2y)-\tfrac{1}{2}\tanh^{2}(y), and φ3∗​(y)=14+cos⁡(y)\varphi_{3}^{\ast}(y)=\tfrac{1}{4}+\cos(y). Writing z=(β1⊤​x,β2⊤​x,β3⊤​x)z=(\beta_{1}^{\top}x,\beta_{2}^{\top}x,\beta_{3}^{\top}x), the four policies are uniform, softmax⁡(2​z)\operatorname{softmax}(2z), softmax⁡(−2​z)\operatorname{softmax}(-2z), and softmax⁡(2​(z2,z3,z1))\operatorname{softmax}(2(z_{2},z_{3},z_{1})). We use m=3​dm=3d at d∈{128,256,512}d\in\{128,256,512\}, with 200 datasets per dimension and the network and training schedule above. Every policy uses the same logged datasets, training trajectories, and Onsager correction, so the comparison changes only the weights used for selection.

Averaging within each dataset over the three nonuniform policies, weighting reduces prediction risk relative to unweighted corrected selection by 0.03150.0315, 0.03110.0311, and 0.03270.0327 across the three dimensions. The corresponding reductions relative to weighted ten-fold CV are 0.02810.0281, 0.02670.0267, and 0.02930.0293. Weighting reduces risk for softmax⁡(2​z)\operatorname{softmax}(2z) and softmax⁡(−2​z)\operatorname{softmax}(-2z) at every dimension, with the larger reduction for the former. For the uniform policy, weighted and unweighted selection coincide. For the cyclically permuted policy, paired intervals for weighted versus unweighted selection contain zero at all three dimensions. The corrected weighted rule has lower mean regret than weighted CV in every policy–dimension setting; its paired interval excludes zero except for softmax⁡(2​z)\operatorname{softmax}(2z) at d=128d=128.

J.5 Value estimation at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio

We use the five m=2​dm=2d settings of Figure 4, with the fitting and selection protocols in Appendix J.2. To compare the selected complement-trained models, we compute their target-policy prediction errors on independent test contexts, conditional on each training complement, and average across folds using held-out fold sizes, using the numerical references in Appendix J.9.

For the bias–variance decomposition, let ere_{r} be a procedure’s policy-value error on dataset rr, with B=200B=200 datasets, and let e¯=B−1​∑rer\bar{e}=B^{-1}\sum_{r}e_{r}. We report empirical squared bias e¯2\bar{e}^{2}, variance B−1​∑r(er−e¯)2B^{-1}\sum_{r}(e_{r}-\bar{e})^{2}, and MSE B−1​∑rer2B^{-1}\sum_{r}e_{r}^{2}. The first two sum exactly to the third before rounding. The variance uses denominator BB and measures variation across complete value estimates with the initializations fixed. Table 3 reports these components and Student tt intervals for the mean squared error; the intervals quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty across datasets.

The bias intervals for ADR and both CF10 procedures contain zero at every dimension. Paired 95%95\% MSE intervals favor ADR over corrected-stopping CF10 at d=256d=256 and over inner-validation CF10 at d=256,2048d=256,2048; the remaining intervals contain zero. Corrected stopping lowers CF10’s MSE point estimate at every dimension, with a paired interval excluding zero only at d=2048d=2048. Prediction-risk improvements need not translate proportionally into value-MSE gains: DR variance combines errors across arms, and cross-fitted estimates also include covariance between folds.

ADR has lower MSE than IPS at d=256,512,2048d=256,512,2048 and than SNIPS at d=2048d=2048, with paired 95%95\% intervals below zero. The remaining intervals contain zero. These comparisons measure finite-sample MSE: with known logging, IPS is unbiased and consistent under the stated moment conditions.

J.6 Risk curves and leave-one-out refitting

Figure 6 shows the two-arm risk curves at d=512d=512 and m=1024m=1024. In later iterations, the training-residual criterion decreases while the test risk rises; the corrected criterion follows the test risk.

We also compare corrected and unadjusted predictions with networks retrained after omitting the evaluated observation. All layers are retrained from the same initialization and with the same learning rates, retaining the original arm denominator NaN_{a} in the loss. We use d∈{128,256,512}d\in\{128,256,512\} and m=2​dm=2d, with 100 independent datasets per dimension and 32 rows sampled uniformly without replacement per dataset. The discrepancy is the root mean squared prediction difference over these rows and datasets.

Figure 7 shows this discrepancy along training. At t=30t=30, the corrected prediction’s root mean squared discrepancy decreases from 0.1770.177 to 0.0860.086 as dd increases from 128128 to 512512, while the unadjusted prediction’s discrepancy remains near 1.171.17.

J.7 Nonuniform logging

We repeat the two-arm Gaussian experiment with context-independent logging probabilities μ⁡(1)∈{0.5,0.25,0.1}\mu(1)\in\{0.5,0.25,0.1\} and μ⁡(2)=1−μ⁡(1)\mu(2)=1-\mu(1). We use d∈{512,1024,2048}d\in\{512,1024,2048\} and m=2​dm=2d, with 200 independent datasets at each setting. The reward links, target policy, initial weights, network architecture, and training schedule remain as specified above, with η=2\eta=2. The uniform-logging reference uses new datasets generated for this comparison.

Each arm’s criterion uses wa​(X)=ν⁡(a∣X)/μ⁡(a)w_{a}(X)=\nu(a\mid X)/\mu(a). We measure error in estimating total target-policy test risk by comparing ∑a=12μ⁡(a)​ℰ^a(ta)\sum_{a=1}^{2}\mu(a)\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t_{a})} with ℛν​(g𝐭)\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\mathbf{t}}), and form the corresponding comparisons for training residuals and cross-validation. The reported RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error over all 31×3131\times 31 pairs of stopping times and datasets. This differs from the arm-wise RMSE in Figure 1. Selection regret uses the total prediction risk ℛν∘\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}, with every rule evaluated on the same full-data training trajectories.

Figure 8 shows that the corrected criterion’s total-risk RMSE and mean selection regret decrease with dimension under each logging distribution. Its empirical mean squared risk-estimation error is smaller than cross-validation’s in all nine settings; the paired 95%95\% Monte Carlo interval for the difference excludes zero except at μ⁡(1)=0.1,d=512\mu(1)=0.1,d=512. The paired selection-regret intervals favor the corrected rule in every setting. For the rare arm at μ⁡(1)=0.1,d=512\mu(1)=0.1,d=512, however, its arm-wise risk RMSE is slightly higher than cross-validation’s, despite the lower total-risk error.

The bottom row of Figure 8 compares DR and ADR at identical full-data models and stopping times selected by the corrected criterion. The correction reduces absolute empirical bias in every setting. For μ⁡(1)=0.1\mu(1)=0.1, the DR bias changes from −0.143-0.143 to −0.193-0.193 as dimension increases from 512512 to 20482048, while the corresponding ADR biases are 0.00040.0004 and 0.00250.0025. All nine ADR bias intervals include zero. This comparison isolates the effect of correcting the predictions used for value estimation.

J.8 Non-Gaussian contexts

We repeat the two-arm experiment at d∈{256,1024,2048}d\in\{256,1024,2048\} and m=2​dm=2d with independent Rademacher coordinates and with independent coordinates distributed as 3/5​T5\sqrt{3/5}\,T_{5}, where T5T_{5} has a Student tt distribution with five degrees of freedom. Both distributions have mean zero and variance one. At each dimension, we retain the Gaussian experiment’s reward links, target policy, initial weights, and training schedule, with independent uniform logging. Each setting uses 200 independent logged datasets.

The upper panels of Figure 9 compare risk estimation under the three context laws. As dimension increases, the corrected criterion’s RMSE decreases from 0.2480.248 to 0.0840.084 for Rademacher contexts and from 0.2440.244 to 0.0880.088 for standardized t5t_{5} contexts. At d=2048d=2048, the corresponding RMSEs are 0.1560.156 and 0.1580.158 for cross-validation, and 1.3351.335 and 1.3341.334 for training residuals. Table 4 compares the resulting stopping decisions on the full-data training trajectories. For both non-Gaussian laws, the corrected rule has smaller mean selection regret than ten-fold cross-validation at every dimension, with the paired 95%95\% intervals below zero.

The lower panels compare DR and ADR at the same full-data models and stopping times selected by the corrected criterion, with the true policy value computed for each context law as in Appendix J.9. The correction reduces absolute empirical bias in all six non-Gaussian settings. At d=2048d=2048, the DR and ADR biases are −0.0191-0.0191 and −0.0034-0.0034 for Rademacher contexts, and −0.0159-0.0159 and −0.0002-0.0002 for standardized t5t_{5} contexts.

J.9 Numerical reference values and uncertainty

Reference test risks are conditional on the fitted models. For Gaussian contexts, we integrate the joint Gaussian vector of signal and policy indices and fitted first-layer projections using two independent scrambled Sobol rules with antithetic points, each containing 2142^{14} points. For non-Gaussian contexts, we average two independent Monte Carlo estimates, each using 16,384 draws and their negatives from the specified context law. The reward-noise contribution is integrated analytically. All reference draws are independent of the logged data and are used only to assess the procedures; they do not enter fitting, selection, or the value estimators.

The true policy value is computed by Gaussian integration, a finite sum over binomial sign counts for Rademacher contexts, or numerical inversion of the signal sums’ characteristic functions for standardized t5t_{5} contexts. Errors of DM, ADM, and cross-arm DM are measured against the average of the two independent numerical references for each fitted model’s value.

For normalized value MSE, we compute σeff2=Var⁡{ψg∗​(X,A,R)}\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}=\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{g^{\ast}}(X,A,R)\} by Gaussian integration and use the true-reward score average 𝒱^or=m−1​∑iψg∗​(Qi)\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{or}}=m^{-1}\sum_{i}\psi_{g^{\ast}}(Q_{i}) as a control variate. Specifically, we average

1+mσeff2​{(𝒱^−𝒱⁡(ν))2−(𝒱^or−𝒱⁡(ν))2}1+\frac{m}{\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}}\left\{(\widehat{\mathcal{V}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu))^{2}-(\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{or}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu))^{2}\right\}

over datasets; the control squared error has mean σeff2/m\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}/m.

All pointwise 95%95\% intervals use Student tt quantiles across independent logged datasets. They describe Monte Carlo uncertainty in performance, rather than uncertainty in policy value from a single dataset. RMSE intervals take square roots of the MSE limits after truncating the lower limit at zero. Comparisons use within-dataset differences; in the target-policy experiment, averages over nonuniform policies are also formed within each dataset before computing intervals.

J.10 Value estimation as sample size outgrows dimension

We compare ADR, DR with ten-fold cross-fitting (CF10), inverse propensity scoring (IPS), and self-normalized IPS (SNIPS) as the number of observations increases relative to the context dimension. We use the two-arm model above and train every reward network with η=1\eta=1 over candidate iterations {0,…,30}\{0,\ldots,30\}. Both corrected-stopping and inner-validation CF10 use the protocols in Appendix J.2; each evaluation fold is excluded from fitting and selection. We first fix d=256d=256 and increase m∈{512,2048,8192,32768}m\in\{512,2048,8192,32768\}. We also increase both dimension and sample-to-dimension ratio along (d,m)∈{(256,2048),(512,8192),(1024,32768)}(d,m)\in\{(256,2048),(512,8192),(1024,32768)\}. Each setting uses 200 independent datasets, except those with m=32768m=32768, which use 100.

We report normalized mean squared error, m​𝔼​[(𝒱^−𝒱⁡(ν))2]/σeff2m\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\mathcal{V}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu))^{2}]/\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}, where σeff2=Var⁡{ψg∗​(X,A,R)}\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}=\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{g^{\ast}}(X,A,R)\}. The normalization σeff2/m\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}/m is the exact MSE of DR using the true reward function, whose normalized MSE is therefore one for every (d,m)(d,m). At a fixed data law, σeff2\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2} is also the classical semiparametric variance bound for known logging and otherwise unrestricted context and reward distributions. We use it here as an oracle reference. We estimate normalized MSE using the control-variate calculation in Appendix J.9.

Figure 5 shows ADR and both CF10 procedures approaching normalized MSE one as sample size outgrows dimension. At (d,m)=(1024,32768)(d,m)=(1024,32768), ADR and corrected-stopping CF10 give 1.0001.000 and 1.0131.013, respectively. At both endpoints with m=32768m=32768, paired ADR-minus-corrected-CF10 intervals contain zero, while ADR’s MSE is lower than IPS and SNIPS with paired intervals below zero.

J.11 Computational cost

ADR requires one full-data training trajectory per arm. Its response recursion adds O⁡(Na​q3​T3)O(N_{a}q^{3}T^{3}) operations and O⁡(Na​T2​q2)O(N_{a}T^{2}q^{2}) storage (Appendix B). Corrected-stopping CF10 repeats this calculation on ten training complements. Table 5 shows that ADR is 5.55.5–8.98.9 times faster in the three benchmark settings. CV and inner-validation CF10 are faster in the smallest setting, while ADR is faster in the larger two.

Both tables report median wall time over five shared datasets per setting, using the two-arm Gaussian model and training settings above, with η=2\eta=2 when m=2​dm=2d and η=1\eta=1 at m=32768m=32768. Each measurement includes training, selection, refitting where required, and final value estimation; common data generation and reference integration are excluded. Runs use one numerical thread, with a separate warm-up excluded. The studies were conducted on different CPUs, so comparisons use the controls within each table.

The single holdouts in Table 6 are faster than ADR. Together with Appendix J.3, this identifies the trade-off: the correction improves risk estimation and stopping selection, while a single holdout costs less. The CV and holdout timings include full-data refitting and raw DR scoring; these procedures compare selection costs, since refitting alone does not correct same-sample DR bias.
